https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqn7: California has served an investigative subpoena on the AI chip designer Nvidia in the wake of a scandal that ended in the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang.

The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney general Rob Bonta, said he is probing whether Nvidia or Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, adding that such actions could violate California law if the company is found to have mislead investors and the public.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said on Thursday.
How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security?
Nvidia has its global headquarters in Santa Clara, California.
Earlier this month, it emerged that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was an executive at the Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.
Some members of the US Congress have urged the Department of Commerce to investigate whether Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Megaspeed has previously said it is aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
Nvidia shares have plummeted 22% since the New York Times reported on the affair in early November.

Earlier this week, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Jensen Huang after the longtime Nvidia boss and co-founder issued a statement saying he would be "honoured" to return, as some tech leaders including Elon Musk campaigned on his behalf.
Huang has acknowledged engaging in extramarital affairs – and left the company last week after reports that he had relationships with subordinates.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj4g: Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
It was during November 2020 that somewhere in San Francisco, a woman called Daniela Amodei phoned a friend, asking for advice.
Daniela oversaw safety and policy at OpenAI, one of the most talked-about AI companies in the world.
But Daniela and her brother Dario - who worked there too - had misgivings over safety levels at OpenAI and thought it could be time to walk away.

So she did what many do when we can't make a decision about something, she phoned a friend. The friend's reply was direct and to the point: "You don't need to be on the phone with me. You already know the answer."
The Amodei siblings and a handful of other colleagues quit. Together, they set up a rival – Anthropic.
Six years on and Anthropic, the maker of leading AI model Claude, has predicted revenues of $52bn in 2026 and $135bn in 2027, according to analyst estimates.

It is selling shares to the public for the first time in what's known as an Initial Public Offering or IPO, aiming for a valuation of an estimated $1.4tn (£1tn), which would propel it straight into the top 10 of the most valuable US companies.
The sale comes at a crucial time when many are wondering whether, amid increasing concern about the potential of AI, the industry's bubble is showing signs of bursting.

Where once investors were "all in" on a technological revolution to rival the railroads, the car, electricity and the internet, some are now hedging their bets, amid arguments that AI prices will be driven down as the technology becomes more common and concerns that a hefty wedge of the AI investment is tech giants investing in each other.

Shares in companies that supply the raw computing power behind AI, like Coreweave and Nebius, have seen their value cut in half while even the mighty Nvidia has lost its crown as the world's most valuable company with its shares down 30% - a staggering $2tn fall in value.
So could the Anthropic IPO reinflate the bubble or will it be remembered as the last gasp of a boom that is heading for a bust?
At an event last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told JPMorgan Chase's CEO Jamie Dimon that his guiding principle was to "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's worth".

The company is selling roughly $81bn worth of shares to the general public and a further $26bn on to other big tech companies. It is comfortably the single biggest money raising event in US corporate history.

It's an old adage that during a gold rush you should buy companies that sell the picks and shovels as opposed to those staking everything on striking gold. In AI's case that's the chip makers, the data centre builders, the energy providers. But Anthropic is arguably the gold itself and this IPO will see what value people put on it, according to Fiona Cincotta from StoneX trading.

"I think the reason that this IPO is so important is basically it's the first ability for the public investors to access a pure play AI trade," she says, adding that previous offerings have been about "other parts of the ecosystem, which are, the semiconductors, the chips, the, data centres. But this is the first time that we were actually able to access the AI provider."
What a company is worth depends almost entirely on predicted future earnings.
It's that calculation that many think presents the sharpest needle to the AI bubble.

Will current and future users of AI be prepared to pay enough to justify the trillions being spent on the chips, data centres, energy and employees, some of whom can command annual salaries of over $100m?

"AI is certainly in a financial bubble. While LLMs [large language models] offer genuine utility and are undoubtedly here to stay, the economics don't add up," said Gary Marcus, Professor Emeritus at New York University and author of Taming Silicon Valley, speaking earlier this year.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6x2: Ex-McDonald's worker: "You need to fix it so it doesn't happen again"
A former McDonald's worker who says a manager failed to protect her when she was being sexualised by customers, has called on the firm to “change the way they treat younger employees”.

Hope, who worked at a branch in the West Midlands in 2023, also told BBC News she saw older colleagues eyeing up 16- and 17-year-old workers, and talking about wanting to sleep with them when they turned 18.
Hope is one of hundreds of workers bringing a discrimination claim against McDonald's. This week, a judge ruled against McDonald's attempt to have their claims struck out, a move that Hope welcomed.
McDonald's said: "Ensuring a safe, respectful and inclusive working environment across our restaurants and offices remains a fundamental priority."
The latest developments come after a BBC investigation in 2023 which heard that workers, some as young as 17, were being groped and harassed.
Last year, McDonald's staff told us they still faced sexual abuse and harassment.
McDonald's boss on abuse claims: 'I don't want to talk about the past'
Hope, who is now 22, says that her branch of McDonalds had a very sexualised, "toxic" environment.
She spoke of a time a manager came up behind her and put his hands on her shoulders. From then on, whenever she saw him coming over, she says she "moved quick" to get away from him.
Another time, she says a manager failed to protect her when she says she was being sexualised and objectified by two customers on a night shift.
Hope says she told the manager what was happening, but he told her to "just suck it up and deal with it".
Her main concern, however, was for the younger teenagers, who she says weren't being looked after.

"You could tell there were other staff members waiting for their 18th birthdays. That sort of like toxic culture where it's like, 'Oh, you know, it's not illegal now.' It was that feeling from quite a few of them," she says.
Hundreds of current and former McDonald's employees are bringing a discrimination claim against the firm.

The fast-food chain had attempted to have the complaints thrown out but this week at the London Central Employment Tribunal, Judge Glennie ruled that 450 cases can go ahead and they are now expected to be heard at the Employment Tribunal in April.
The BBC understands that these relate to indirect discrimination, not sexual harassment.
Hope told us she was not taking part in the legal case for money, saying they didn't know if they were going to get anything.
Instead, she said it was to try and "change the way they treat younger employees".

"It's going to change the way they treat allegations. It's going to shake up the whole internal process and make life easier for the kids who are now having their first jobs. And it's going to make it a lot safer, I think, as well. And that's something you can't put a price on, the safety of the young these days.''
She also accused McDonald's of trying to "delay the inevitable" by attempting to have the claims thrown out.
"And the judge quite rightly looked at them and said: 'No. We're not going to do that.'"
The claims were presented by law firm Leigh Day, which is acting for the current and former employees.
The claims focus on the vulnerability of young or female workers in the workplace and follow allegations of widespread harassment and discrimination across McDonald's restaurants in the UK.

Leigh Day partner Kiran Daurka told the BBC: "We're really delighted that the judge has found that these claims can go forward to a full hearing. It's really important for access to justice that these cases are heard."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw8d: Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of online woes.
Retailers promise bargains - but the sheer number of offers can leave us feeling no closer to finding the best deal.
It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.
But are they any good at finding Black Friday deals? We had a go ourselves a week ahead of the big day.
Figures suggest relatively few UK shoppers currently go to AI tools for help.
A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries found the UK ranked second-last in the proportion of people who said they had used AI to help them shop.
Crucially, 36% of respondents who said they would be shopping around Black Friday didn't plan to use an AI tool at all.
But the survey suggested a growing number of people were considering it - and tech firms have released features to capitalise on this.
Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.
In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.
But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.
We asked four models to find a 55-inch TV deal, using the free versions of many of the most popular tools.
While this was not a rigorous scientific test, the experience we had produced mixed results.
Its top pick was a Hisense TV on Chinese retailer Joybuy's website, on sale for £499 down from £649.
The next recommendation was a 55-inch TCL-branded TV, but a sidebar showed prices for the 50-inch version, from £379 to £814.
Option three was the same Hisense TV as before, but for full price at £649 from John Lewis and Richer Sounds.
This was the "best safer purchase" according to ChatGPT, as the sites offered longer guarantee periods.
But clicking on the links did not go well. Both retailers said the TV was no longer listed online.
The fourth option was equally fruitless - another TCL TV, at full price, £150 over our budget and not available online.
At the bottom, ChatGPT served one last offer - "one OLED option to compare" - for a £1,100 LG TV that was marked as "Ad" .
Claude produced the shortest answer of all the models we tested, and unlike the others, it did not give much detail on the specifications of each model.
Instead, it seemed to base its results on a small number of reviews published online.
But when we clicked on the links, they sent us to two dead pages on the Richer Sounds website.
Some other links led to year-old round-ups of Black Friday 2025 deals.
Claude was not very enthusiastic about its other two recommendations due to a lack of independent reviews - calling one "a decent option" but saying it "wouldn't pick" the other.
It also listed two Samsung TVs, but it told us not to buy them, with one "over budget and not clearly better than the TCLs".
We were left wondering why it even mentioned them in the first place.
Different AI model, same TV manufacturers - albeit different Hisense and TCL models to the previous chatbots' recommendations.
Gemini generated a table comparing four different models, but offered no links to the stores it named, so we searched for them ourselves.
The prices for one TCL TV were correct at £649, but it was sold out at one of the named retailers.
It said the other TCL model was available from Argos and Currys for £539 - correct for Argos, but when we checked Currys, it was £60 more expensive.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwz0: Sean Cairncross (left) was appointed by the Trump administration
The top cyber-security official in the US government is leaving his post after a little over a year in the job.

White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired after losing the confidence of the White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, according CBS, the BBC's US news partner. Asked about his removal on Friday, President Donald Trump said it was because he was not "good enough".
His firing comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors.
US officials said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks but the blackouts had sparked scrutiny from members of Congress who demanded a clearer explanation of what went wrong.

There has been no official confirmation of the removal of Cairncross but Secretary of State Marco Rubio posted on X , external to say Department of Defense chief information officer Kirsten Davies was the new national cyber director.

The news, first reported by Axios , external , follows security concerns, including the ability of advanced AI models - mostly from US companies - to discover vulnerabilities which humans would not be able to find on their own.
Earlier this week, Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the outages were connected, adding "we are not under systemic attack".
But the fact that so many have happened in quick succession has left some people worried about the safety of the tech which is heavily relied on in all aspects of daily life.
Hacks, AI or just overdue updates - why have there been so many outages?
Cairncross was previously a lawyer in the Republican Party, before becoming the chief operating officer of the Republican National Committee.
In the first Trump administration, he was part of the team of the White House chief of staff.
He later worked in the private sector, before returning to government in August 2025.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckq6: The Dutch privacy watchdog, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), has told people not to buy smart glasses, saying they can get things dangerously wrong.

It said in its tests of six glasses available on the Dutch market, the devices advised a user on how to date a child, misread medicine instructions, and claimed to have called an ambulance when they had not.
While the AP is advising people not to buy the smart glasses, it stopped short of calling for them to be banned from sale.
The authority is not revealing which glasses it tested, saying only that prices ranged from under €100 (£84) to over €500 and originated from different continents.

The research follows growing concerns about privacy risks associated with smart glasses, in particular the misuse of the tech to film women without consent , or to record in places where filming is usually prohibited such as healthcare settings.
Meta, a leading seller of the glasses, recently released a version without a camera with some commentators suggesting this was a response to the privacy backlash.
It is unknown if the investigation included Meta's glasses. The AP told the BBC it would not name the products it tested.
The BBC has approached Meta, TCL and HTC - all major manufacturers of smart glasses - for comment.
Previously, these firms have been keen to highlight positive uses of smart glasses.
Meta has highlighted the assistance they can provide to people with visual impairments. Its smart glasses use AI to describe things in the wearer's environment or to read text.
The AP recognises the glasses can be valuable for people who need help to understand their surroundings.
But for these users, it argues it is particularly important that AI is reliable.
AP said in its testing of the unnamed brands, it found the advice given could be wrong.

During a simulated emergency in which CPR resuscitation advice was requested, the AP found one pair of glasses claimed several times an ambulance was on the way - but emergency services had not been contacted.
It said the AI also made child protection errors, with potentially serious consequences.
One pair of glasses gave dating advice to an adult who indicated a romantic interest in a minor.
The glasses also made errors when reading instructions inside medicine packages, as well as with interpreting severe weather warnings.
And the AP was concerned smart glasses could be used to secretly film people, highlighting the ease with which lights, which warn that a device is recording, could be obscured.
It said with some glasses these lights could be covered with tape and they would still work, despite some manufacturers claiming they would not function.
Meanwhile, in some glasses, the AP found serious security flaws which meant someone nearby could connect without permission, view recordings, or even operate the camera remotely.
It warned data recorded by the glasses was often exported outside the EU.
In February, reports revealed outsourced workers were able to view sensitive content recorded on Meta smart glasses
Meta said at the time such workers might sometimes review content, including video and images, in order to help improve its AI .
It said it took the protection of people's data very seriously, and was constantly refining its efforts and tools in that area, and would filter it first to blur faces in images.
The AP investigation was not primarily focused on data protection - instead it was concerned with algorithms and AI.

In the UK Paul Arnold, chief executive of privacy watchdog the Information Commission, who has a severe visual impairment has previously stressed the complexity of the argument , external around smart glasses.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c674: Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, has raised a record $81bn (£62bn) in a stock market debut that will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.

A surge of investor appetite to buy shares in the loss-making business meant more stock was sold than originally planned. Anthropic's shares have been priced at $83, up from the proposed $70-$78 range.
Shares will begin trading later on Thursday in New York, valuing the five year-old firm at around $1.5 trillion.
The flotation is being seen as a crucial test for fast-growing AI sector. Anthropic is the first purely AI-focused firm to publicly sell its shares.
Vast amounts of money have been poured into AI infrastructure and the development of AI based tools. But questions are being raised over whether and when those investments will pay off.
The seven founders, who set up Anthropic up in 2021, will become multi-billionaires immediately.

The company's $1.5tn estimated valuation is on a "diluted" basis, a broader reflection of the firm's value that takes things like employee stock options into account. On a basic share count Anthropic is worth about $1.1tn, more valuable than Walmart and Samsung but less than Tesla and Meta.
But strong demand could push its share price, and overall valuation, higher, once shares are publicly traded.

Anthropic's revenues have ballooned in the last year, to $33bn in the nine months to September this year, as the market for its tools, designed to speed up processes including coding, writing and digesting information, has grown.
But net losses have also increased, reaching $104bn for the same period, according to the company's IPO document.

Leah Bramwell from Canaccord Wealth said there had been strong interest in Anthropic shares "across the board" including both institutional and retail - that is private individual - investors, which she said suggested it was not simply a "retail-driven frenzy into into AI names".

In total Anthropic could raise $107bn. Over $81bn comes from the public share sale, with an additional $26bn from separate investments from a group of tech firms including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.
Anthropic could raise a further $12bn through an additional provision, which is normal practice, to permit further shares to be sold if demand is very high.
Elon Musk's SpaceX raised an initial $75bn in its IPO in June this year.
The company soared in value when it joined the Nasdaq, reaching $2.2tn, although in the weeks that followed, the share price fell.
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei co-founded firm five years ago

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year. Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology.
While there is excitement around Anthropic's listing, there is also some concern from investors about its future ability to generate profits in a competitive area.

Yang Wang, a principle analyst at Counterpoint Research, said the central issue was whether it could "keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.
However, the share sale would give investors "direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity", Wang said.
Anthropic was started by seven former OpenAI employees, led by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei.
Dario Amodei has been outspoken about the risks posed by AI, amounting in his view to a possible threat to human existence.
The company has called for a slowdown in the development of AI, and a greater focus on safeguards while forging ahead with plans to grow quickly and boost its financing through the public markets.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6z7: After years of anticipation and delays, as well as controversy around worker rights, Grand Theft Auto 6 has completed its phased worldwide release and is available to gamers everywhere, including the UK.
There has been near universal praise from critics, with review aggregator Metacritic calculating its average score at 99 out of 100 based on 150 reviews. , external
Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has held the top spot since 1998 - but Metacritic confirmed to the BBC that this has now officially been overtaken.
GTA 6 is set to become one of the world's most popular entertainment products ever, with fans booking time off work, and schools warning students not to bunk off.
Some schools have reminded parents and pupils to prioritise study over the game, which has an 18 rating , external for "strong graphic violence, strong sexual themes and use of illegal drugs".
One school in Essex incentivised pupils to attend with prizes such as vouchers, Christmas dinners and a pass to skip the lunch queue.
The UK rating means it can only be legally sold to an adult. It does not stop an adult letting their child play the game - instead it is meant to inform their decision.
It's the game that shocked and thrilled the world: Grand Theft Auto. As a new installment is released in 2026, go deep into the history of the game with rapper Bugzy Malone.
The game, set in the fictional US state of Leonida, follows two protagonists, Lucia and Jason, through the seedy underbelly of America after an "easy score goes wrong".
It was released at midnight in all the countries it is available in, which meant New Zealanders were the first to access it.
"The graphics are great. Even from the set-up and credits, it's feeling pretty good," Aleana Fernando, who lives in Auckland, New Zealand, told BBC Newsbeat soon after she started playing.
Once the game was released at midnight UK time, gamers were equally enthralled by the game's graphics and attention to detail.
Charlie Wood from London said he had "already laughed at the dialogue before even stepping into the gameplay".
About 30 minutes into playing in Leonida, he said it was "most definitely worth the wait".
Meanwhile in Germany, Timur told the BBC he was impressed by how lifelike the game was.
"It really feels like a life simulation with the amount of in-game encounters," he said.
The Guardian's Keza MacDonald , external was impressed by the relationship between the main characters.
"GTA has never been particularly kind to women... there is still a lot of sexism in GTA VI's world, but now we have Lucia to react to it," she said.
"This is the first GTA in which I have felt the women are treated as people, not only Lucia but also the many other female characters in the story".
From the memes to the music - from the controversies to the culture - you have your say on GTA 6 with Newsbeat's Jordan Kenny and De-Graft Mensah.

After GTA 5 became one of the most successful entertainment products of all time - with estimates of net profits soaring as high up as $10bn (£7.6bn) - anticipation could not be higher for the sixth instalment.
Makers Rockstar North, headquartered in Edinburgh, delayed the release twice, saying it needed extra months to finish the game with the level of polish fans had come to "expect and deserve".
The company was also set back by hacks and leaks of its unfinished version.
On Monday, 21-year-old Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, pleaded guilty to the Rockstar Games hack and a handful of others which he carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old with the hacking gang Lapsus$.
He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished and hugely anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm9q: Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.

The Tesla and SpaceX chief executive was the election's top individual donor , giving $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.
Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.
Democrats won control of both chambers in the US Congress, flipping both swing seats and making historic gains in places that have for decades been controlled by Republicans.
The election was seen as a bruising defeat for Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living in the US.
Musk was speaking virtually , external at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.
"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.
He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."
This marks a major shift in tone by Musk, who has previously been seen wearing a Maga hat.
"I'm not just Maga, I'm dark, gothic Maga," he joked at a Trump rally in 2024.

For several months at the start of Trump's second term in the White House, Musk served as an unpaid "special government employee" and Senior Advisor to the President, leading the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) to cut government spending.
In October 2026, the Pentagon named Musk as a co-lead of a future of warfare study called Project Meridian, while he continued to travel with and advise Trump.
Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.
The large number of Republican losses could have implications for Musk and his businesses.
Democrats coming into power in both the Senate and House of Representatives have pledged greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the building of controversial data centres.

In Georgia, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the newly elected Democrat governor promised to limit the rollout of the massive buildings , as well as the tax breaks tech companies often get to build them.
Democratic lawmakers have also suggested that SpaceX, which has gained an estimated $10bn in new government contracts since Trump was re-elected, should be investigated.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/formula1/art: Max Verstappen (left) and George Russell (right) will start on the front row in the Las Vegas Grand Prix
The Las Vegas Grand Prix will start with two drivers on the front row who dislike each other - and after qualifying one said of the other that "somebody has got to stand up to that guy".
"That guy" is Max Verstappen, who starts his Red Bull from pole position. The driver criticising him is Mercedes' George Russell, who lines up second.
Both were promoted after the fastest qualifier, new world champion Kimi Antonelli, was demoted by a five-place grid penalty for exceeding his engine allocation for the season.
Russell's beef stemmed from an incident in final practice, in which Verstappen overtook the Mercedes on the Las Vegas Strip, then veered in front of him into Turn 14.

Russell, unhappy with the Dutchman's behaviour, dived down the Red Bull's inside on braking for the corner, got alongside, and then made his displeasure known by pushing Verstappen wide, the two cars making light contact.
They were called to the stewards to discuss the incident. Verstappen was given a warning having been found to have made an "unpredictable change of direction under braking".

After qualifying, Russell told Sky Italia: "I think the warning was fine. There's nothing in the rules to say that you cannot overtake someone who is starting their lap but when you do this, you are screwing this person over.

"He does this week in, week out, with many drivers. Everybody accepts it and I am not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they are bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody has got to stand up to that guy."
Russell's comments were not put to Verstappen as he had finished his media commitments by the time they emerged into wider knowledge in Las Vegas.
Asked about the incident in the official news conference, Verstappen said: "Nothing happened."
When Verstappen spoke to the Dutch media, he was again reluctant to be drawn on it.
But asked whether it gave him extra motivation to beat Russell in the race, he said: "I don't need any extra motivation."
George Russell and Max Verstappen battling for track position during final practice in Las Vegas

These two have history. This incident is almost exactly two years since they fell out in public following a row at the Qatar Grand Prix where Verstappen felt Russell had stepped over the line to get him a penalty that demoted him from pole position.
They exchanged insults. Russell, in remarks that echo those from Las Vegas, said: "People have been bullied by Max for years now."
That was just the latest in a series of incidents - after a clash in Azerbaijan in 2022, Verstappen called Russell "Princess George" in a spat the Briton called "a little bit pathetic".
And then there was the 2025 Spanish Grand Prix. Late in the race, with Verstappen struggling with his tyres, they banged wheels as Russell attempted an overtake.

Verstappen retained the position after going off track and after being told by his team to hand the position to Russell, he moved over for the Mercedes and then appeared back on its inside and made contact with it.
He was penalised 10 seconds for that, and the following day issued a public apology for his behaviour.
Verstappen goes off track after clashing with Russell in Las Vegas
All this certainly adds a hefty dose of extra spice to a race which, frankly, needs it.

This is the first of three 'dead rubbers' to close the season now both championships have been settled. There is little to fight for, and very little enthusiasm in the paddock for the final two races in the war-torn Middle East.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/taekwondo/ar: Athlete who lost hand saving friends in attack 'would do it again'
When an Islamist militant group threw a grenade at 11-year-old Ismael 'Ox' Oumarou and his friends in Niger, he didn't run away from it, he ran towards it.
He "just grabbed it", but while he was trying to throw it away from his friends, it detonated.
A promising taekwondo athlete who had taught himself by peering through the window of the local dojo, he lost his right hand in the explosion.
Everyone around him wrote off his sporting ambitions, no-one would imagine him one day at a World Championships, let alone representing the USA.
But Ox, who'd had to work since he was six and had been homeless at nine, has always known how to fight.

Raised by his grandma in rural Niger, he lived with about 40 other people and had been exposed to a lot of fighting as a youngster which he "thought was normal" and had been expelled from several schools.
His father was briefly on the scene when he was five but Ox says he would kick and hit him until he bled and also kick his mother.

Sent out to the streets of the capital city Niamey to sell water or anything he could to "make money just to be able to eat", Ox would go past a dojo to watch and copy people doing martial arts to learn "a way to survive" and fight back.
He began to dream of being like Jackie Chan and his kung-fu movie characters and began to teach himself some of the skills.

"I thought that, one day, I'm going to become strong like him. I'm going to go in a small village, somewhere far away from everybody. I'm going to get strong, then come back in my village, beat everybody," the now 25-year-old tells BBC Sport.
It was this, though, that led him to be kicked out of his grandma's home at the age of nine, with Ox saying he "started attacking people and fighting them in the street".
One day during a street fight a man approached him and said: "You have so much anger in you. I'm going to put you in something that can be useful for you."
It turned out he was a taekwondo coach, and so Ox began training with him, developing his skills and started to dream of becoming "the best at taekwondo in the world".
Ismael Ox won a 'best athlete' award at a tournament in Ghana

Ox says jihadist group Boko Haram, which kidnapped more than 200 schoolgirls from the village of Chibok in neighbouring Nigeria in 2014, were in his village trying to "take young girls and kill people" when they threw the grenade.
"I don't really know what I was thinking, I was just young and tried to get it away from everybody," says Ox. "But right now, I would do it again, even tomorrow."
Ox spent two weeks in hospital and left "with a lot of anger" inside him because of the uncertainty of how he would return to his new sport.
There were a lot of people, including family, who thought Ox returning to fighting after losing his hand was him "just talking nonsense".
"Who do you think you're going to be able to fight with one hand?" they would ask.

Perhaps they should not have doubted his self-belief. This was, after all, a child who when he watched his first taekwondo championship turned to his friend and declared he would one day beat the champion.
Ox tried to enter able-bodied tournaments but was turned away and began to think about stopping. But he loved fighting too much and eventually heard about Para-taekwondo.
"I didn't know anything about Para-taekwondo at the time, and even the people I trained with in Niger didn't know about it. I just wanted to fight," he says.
He used all the money he had to travel to competitions, sometimes having to sleep in the event venues as he could not afford accommodation.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/boxing/artic: Lauren Price hopes to fight on bigger stages as her career continues
Lauren Price dominated Michaela Kotaskova to seal her place in history by becoming undisputed world welterweight champion.

Price, 32, took an unanimous, shut-out decision and the acclaim of the crowd to add the WBO title to her collection and become the first Welsh fighter to claim the accolade of holding all four major world titles.
Already an Olympic champion and world champion from her amateur days, it further underlined her claim as being among the very best in boxing.
But the way in which she did it, extending a perfect professional record to 11 wins from her 11 fights, suggested there could yet be more to come.
Price v Kotaskova: Watch undisputed title fight after Edwards v McGregor
Price won every round from every judge in front of a partisan Cardiff crowd, producing an unrelenting pace that punished her opponent at every opportunity.
Although Price could not force a stoppage, there was never any doubt she had done enough against an opponent full of stamina and stubbornness.
Kotaskova, beaten only once, but never stopped in her career, showed real heart but had no answer to Price's expertise.
The Tokyo gold medal winner could celebrate even before the final bell sounded, climbing the corner ropes and into the record books.
It was lapped up by a sell-out Utilita Arena crowd who excitedly acknowledged the achievement and the moment.
Wales has produced 14 world champions, some of them genuine greats.
They include, of course, Joe Calzaghe who so often graced this venue with successful defence after successful defence of his super-middleweight crown.
He never reached undisputed status, though he was able to cross the capital city to go from arena to stadium champion.

That is the next challenge for Price, claiming before she left the ring that more is to come while talk immediately turned to five-weight world champion Claressa Shields as a stadium fight next summer.
That is for the future, but this was a night for history - with the calibre of some of the former boxers in the stands a nod to that.
Champions know champions. Five Welsh world title winners were in the capital to watch their compatriot do something never been done before.
From Cinderella Man Steve Robinson and Barry Jones, to the more recent Joe Cordina, who may still be eyeing a stadium return of his own in the coming weeks.
All have been proud to fly the flag, but perhaps none have worn it quite as much on their sleeve - or shorts - as Price has done.
Here, entering to the strains of a Welsh male voice choir, the atmosphere moved from Friday night in a city centre to full-blooded patriotism.
The anthem stirred so much Kotaskova couldn't help but raise an eyebrow before stepping out of her corner.
From then, she had no time to savour the moment let alone consider become an opportunity the Czech Republic's first world champion.
She felt flurries of punches from the first moments and struggled with the unrelenting pace set by the champion.
Steely-eyed, Price refused to allow a breath and, while Kotaskova continued to try and come onto the front foot, she was met by angry, but calculated attacks.
Kotaskova's problems only increased when she was cut in the fifth round, the hooks from the home fighter providing no let up.
At one point in the seventh, Kotaskova took a shot so fierce she almost turned her back to say no more, but still she came and still Price went hunting with hooks.
She could not find the decisive blow, finally letting the tempo slip, and even enjoying the final seconds as she accepted she had done more than enough to win and win a place in boxing history.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cricket/arti: Cricket Australia has "unequivocally rejected" the suggestion that captain Pat Cummins' integrity has been compromised by the sandpaper scandal.
On Saturday CA gave its "unanimous support" to Cummins, and he said he would take part in the independent forum set up for players and staff.

Cummins has faced claims to step down as captain after Cameron Bancroft's detailed testimony supported claims made by Usman Khawaja that the entire Australia team knew of the plan to tamper with the ball during a Test against South Africa in Cape Town in 2018.
CA and Cummins met this week, with the former saying it was "determined to steward Australian cricket through this very difficult time with diligence and patience and to listen and learn".
"We've expressed our support to Pat and our concern for everyone impacted by the events of the 2018 tour of South Africa," CA said.

"We have learned from that experience and are proud of the team and the culture Pat and other leaders in the team have fostered over the past eight years and unequivocally reject any implication that Pat's integrity has been compromised."
CA chief executive Todd Greenberg said Cummins has been an "exemplary leader" in his five years as captain.
"He has consistently spoken and articulated what happened back in 2018 in his version of events. Nothing's changed. Thus, nothing's changing with our captaincy," Greenberg told BBC Sport.

Greenberg acknowledged that people's version of events "directly contradict" each other but said Cummins has "not moved one inch" from his story, giving the same account now as he did when interviewed the day after the Cape Town Test in 2018.
Cummins is due to lead Australia in the opening match of a four-Test series against New Zealand starting on 9 December in Perth.
The pace bowler reiterated his stance that he had no involvement in or knowledge of the sandpaper plot during a 68-minute news conference last week.
Cummins has said he will attend the forum that has been set up by CA for players and staff to share their version of events.
"All of the players and staff I have spoken with are very keen to go and to have their say.
"There will be a lot of difficult conversations, but that is what's needed.
"Otherwise, from this point, captaining the Australian team in Perth will be my focus and priority."
The row over the sandpaper saga, one of the biggest controversies in Test history, has engulfed Australian sport since Khawaja's claims emerged two weeks ago.
In 2018 Bancroft was banned for nine months and captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner for a year after Bancroft was caught rubbing sandpaper on the ball during the third Test at Newlands.

Khawaja, who retired from international cricket this year, wrote in his autobiography that all the Australia team knew and should have taken responsibility. He has since been supported by Warner and bowlers Chadd Sayers and Jon Holland.
Cummins' said in his news conference that Khawaja's assertions were "100% wrong" and "nonsense".
Fox Sports has taken Khawaja and Warner off commentary duties for the next few weeks.
Fox Sports managing director Steve Crawley said it was "unfair" to put them in a position where it would be "difficult to focus on the game".
In backing Cummins, Greenberg said he was not accusing Bancroft, Khawaja and Warner of lying.
"I'm not putting someone's version of events over somebody else's," he said.
"I don't think they're lying, but I can't tell you what they know and what they don't know. I can only take on face value what they're saying."
Greenberg said it was an "almost impossible" task to put together the truth of what happened given people have different recollections of what happened.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: Ben White's crucial goal against world champions Spain on Sunday will not be forgotten by England fans for a long time.

A smart finish to cap a flowing Three Lions move gave Thomas Tuchel's men an almost unbelievable 3-0 lead in Madrid . They hung on - just - meaning White will always be remembered as the player who scored that winner.

But, for White, the moment represented more than just a goal. It signalled a dramatic turnaround in fortunes for his international career - just four years after many thought his England days were over.
The Arsenal defender has had a tough time on the international stage to say the least.
He left the World Cup in 2022 after a disagreement with then assistant manager Steve Holland and made himself unavailable during the rest of Gareth Southgate's time in charge.

Since returning to England duty in March under Tuchel, the 29-year-old has now established himself as arguably England's best right-back - despite facing jeers from sections of his own fans for his decision to leave that camp.

The defender, who initially arrived at Arsenal from Brighton as a centre-back, has had an excellent start to the season, having played a crucial part in the Gunners' first title win for 22 years last time out.

It hasn't been straightforward for him at Arsenal either though. White has had to navigate his own injury problems and at one point when the defender was struggling for fitness, there was talk that the Gunners should look at moving him on.
But White has battled back and even dealt with competition from Jurrien Timber to remain one of Arsenal 's key players.
60 minutes of perfection, 30 minutes of chaos - an England win for the ages
"I think just obviously people don't know the full story, because I never said anything and won't put anyone under the bus", White said before the England win over Spain.
The 29-year-old is keen to put the well-covered departure from the World Cup in Qatar behind him.
After his long absence from playing for England, some supporters did not believe that White should return.
His first appearance at Wembley since that incident in a friendly against Uruguay in March was booed by some supporters, loud enough for Tuchel to be asked about it after the match.
That game in itself was dramatic for White, who scored the opening goal for England before giving away the penalty that saw the Three Lions draw 1-1 with Uruguay.
White, who missed the World Cup with injury, had been expecting the reaction from some fans. But he is used to proving himself and changing the perception around him.
Tuchel was keen to back his player and said in the build-up to the Spain game that he hoped that the chapter was closed on White being booed by his own supporters.
"Obviously a bit tricky and not straightforward, but yes, it's obviously amazing to be here now." White said of his return to England.
White said in that same interview that he would make the same decision again that he did at the World Cup, but it was now time to move on.
His displays show exactly where his mindset is for his country.
He played the final 12 minutes in England's win over Croatia at Wembley before being brought into the starting line-up for England's toughest match of the November international break against Spain.
This new era of England is being dubbed Tuchel 2.0 and White firmly seems to be part of it.
Chelsea defender Reece James is out with injury. He is a big favourite of Tuchel's but cannot be relied upon for every game due to injuries.
White is a key player for the Premier League champions, reliable in defence and a threat in attack while being physically imposing. There is a lot for Tuchel to like.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/: There is a string of symbols tattooed on to Will Stuart's left foot.
A circle, two triangles, an up arrow, another circle, R1, L2, an up arrow, a triangle, and, finally L1 three times.
England and British and Irish Lions star Stuart is indelibly, if jokingly, stamped with a Grand Theft Auto cheat code, , external which gives your character maximum in-game sex appeal.
In the absence of the injured Stuart and his cheat code at the start of this year, England certainly lost their mojo.
They had a terrible Six Nations. They were comfortably held at bay by South Africa. Five straight defeats ramped up pressure on the squad and their staff.
Stuart has now returned from a ruptured Achilles tendon and, with him, so has England's swagger.
They are ranked top of the Nations Championship for points scored and entries into the opposition 22m. Their attack has shown dexterity of a card sharp, with the sophistication of a socialite.
Those are the sort of intricacies needed to befuddle the best defences.
"We want England to support us. We want to bring joy to them," said head coach Steve Borthwick this week.
So far, this autumn, that objective has been achieved. Twickenham has been seduced by two charismatic displays which have been high on entertainment, if low on jeopardy.
New Zealand are sore. Last weekend's defeat by Wales - their first in 73 years - stung. Coach Dave Rennie's public accusation that the players had "let the country down" will have salted wounds.
He may well have said the same of the insipid performance the team put up in a 33-19 defeat by England last year, under his predecessor Scott Robertson.
The Rennie-ssance overseen by their new boss, with wins over France, Ireland and South Africa in his first few months in charge, has given way to talk of looming crisis.
New Zealand have lost four of their past seven matches after going down 3-1 in the 'Greatest Rivalry' series against South Africa and losing to Wales last weekend
All Black backs are up hard against a brick wall. And big names - Will Jordan, Jordie Barrett, Cam Roigard and Damian McKenzie - are back to blast their way out of a hole.
One of the benefits of being in the northern half of the Nations Championship is a steadier supply of fodder.
Fiji and Japan - the two teams invited to fill out the southern half of the new competition - have won only one of 10 games between them and have a combined points difference of minus 257.
Despite last week's reverse, New Zealand - along with world champions South Africa - are where southern-hemisphere quality is concentrated. And where England's revival will be truly stress-tested.
The comeback of Stuart, and others, has been key for England.
England made a clean sweep of their last autumn campaign, with a high-calibre set of replacements key.
Any lingering final-quarter hopes for the visitors were flushed out by England's depth on the bench.
Stuart is playing the front-row super-sub once again. Fin Baxter - another long-time injury absentee - starts at loosehead, to allow England to rotate between two top-class front rows.

George Martin - an old-school second row enforcer who is recently back from his own 14-month lay-off - is on a bench, also including Henry Pollock and Marcus Smith, loaded with stardust and points to prove.
George Furbank, whose running threat and playmaking ability from deep adds an extra dimension to attack, starts at full-back after a rotten run of knocks and set-backs.

Captain Maro Itoje seems rejuvenated by a summer off. Ollie Chessum is perhaps in the best form of his life. Seb Atkinson - still only eight caps into his Test career - has brought a mix of hard running and soft skills to 12.
Wales will play Australia for the 50th time at Principality Stadium

It was the chance to finally claim the scalp of a southern hemisphere big gun. The opportunity to make a statement ahead of the 2027 World Cup that they are capable of beating any of the top teams on their day.
Wales will now attempt to claim a hat-trick of Cardiff wins in the Nations Championship on Saturday night after the most unlikely of victories against New Zealand.
It is a success that has changed the November narrative. Rather than "can they do it?", the question is now "can they back it up?".
Listen live on BBC Radio Wales, BBC Radio Cymru and Sports Extra on BBC Sounds
Wales' win against the All Blacks was arguably the biggest shock in international rugby since Japan beat South Africa in Brighton in the 2015 World Cup.
What is rarely mentioned is that the Brave Blossoms - hindered by a farcical four-day turnaround - failed to back that up when thumped by Scotland in Gloucester in their following game.
Japan caused another surprise on home soil in 2019 when they beat Ireland and that time they did follow up with victories against Samoa and Scotland.
"It's a real test of our mental and physical preparation," admitted head coach Tandy.
"We can't assume that because one scoreboard went our way, everything is fixed.
"We have to double-down on performance, how we recover, how we train and executing the core areas of our game.
"We have to be at our absolute best to compete with the Aussies."
Tandy frequently talks about performance rather than results, yet this is an occasion where an ugly victory would do.
Wales' belief has soared but they remain slight underdogs for the fixture.
The odds are not as generous as last week's 20-1, but Tandy's men are hunting another scalp.
They are ninth in the world rankings and the Wallabies are seventh.
"It's not do or die, but they will want the performance and result," former Wales hooker Scott Baldwin told the Scrum V podcast.
"None of us expected the New Zealand win, it was one for the ages. If they perform anywhere near that then they win quite comfortably.
"After you have beaten the All Blacks, you go into the Six Nations believing you can beat anyone."
Wales enjoyed their moment, dealt with the acclaim, soaked in the social media reactions and fulfilled plenty of extra media requests.
But they were back in for training on Monday afternoon - business as usual(ish).
"I don't think anyone really felt a sore body until Tuesday because of the emotion and riding the weekend," said captain Dewi Lake.
"There might have been some things the coaches pulled here and there, some minutes off the clock, but the intensity, the challenge, the effort has been exactly the same.
"We've spoken about kicking on from this and to do that you just have to keep pushing."
Wales can go three from three in Cardiff and would then travel to London hunting a perfect November in a fixture likely to be against Japan.
Warren Gatland's class of 2018 are the only team to have enjoyed an autumn clean sweep.
Wales do not want to go from the biggest of highs against New Zealand - something that even the Grand Slam greats could not achieve - to a deflating home loss.
"When you come down off a high like that it is important you get the messaging right," said Gloucester hooker Lake.

Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli was fastest in qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix but a grid penalty will hand pole position to Red Bull's Max Verstappen.
Antonelli, running at the back of the pack of cars in qualifying and maximising his tow, beat Verstappen by 0.258 seconds.
But the new world champion has a five-place grid penalty for using more than permitted number of engine components and will start sixth.
The Italian's team-mate George Russell was just 0.073secs behind Verstappen and will start alongside the Dutchman on the front row.
McLaren's Lando Norris qualified fourth, and will start third, ahead of Red Bull's Isack Hadjar.
Both Ferraris were eliminated in the second session and qualified 11th and 12th with Charles Leclerc ahead of Lewis Hamilton.
Each will be promoted a place by a 10-place penalty for McLaren's Oscar Piastri, who qualified seventh.
Racing Bulls' rookie Arvid Lindblad, sixth fastest, is the last driver to be promoted as a result of Antonelli's penalty.
Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson will start seventh with Alpine's Pierre Gasly eighth and Franco Colapinto ninth.
'Somebody has to stand up to that guy' - and Russell has his chance in Vegas
Antonelli's final run did not start auspiciously as he and Russell became tangled up with the Alpines and Racing Bulls as they sought the best track position to optimise the slipstream effect.
Antonelli ended up the last driver to run and made it to the line with only one second to spare before the chequered flag, one second behind Lindblad.

Normally, being so close to the car in front would be a compromise but in Las Vegas it magnified the tow effect and Antonelli leapt to the front. "That was all the tow," he said over the radio after being told he was on pole.
"Starting the lap, I was only one second behind the car in front and I thought I was screwed," he said. "But the tow is so powerful here."

Verstappen, who has won two of the three Las Vegas Grands Prix, said: "I have been struggling with some weird issues that were also in the car in Brazil and just trying to get my head around how to deal with that.
"In qualifying we managed to make it work. Had a solid qualifying. My first lap in qualifying was pretty much as good as it could be with the tow, so to be on the front row is good for us.
"It was solid in the corners, and you have a bit of dirty air, but it is insane how much you gain on the straights."
Russell had looked in the running for the pole, but was happy with his session despite missing out.
"Overall it's been a very solid session and a solid day," he said.
"I wanted to be on pole but I am probably more pleased with the performance than in Mexico when I was on the front row.
"Kimi did a great job and he probably thought it wasn't going to work out so well being so close but with the tow it worked out."
In four grands prix in Las Vegas, Lewis Hamilton's best qualifying result is 10th
Leclerc and Hamilton were separated by 0.056 seconds and both had tales of woe that explained their early exit - but very different ones.

Leclerc said: "Just a very poor qualifying. We are losing one second in the straights which makes it difficult enough already, and then I did a mistake when I had to put the lap in in Q2, following multiple mistakes we have done as a team and this we need to look at because it builds a lot of frustration that doesn't help.
"But in the end the mistake is on me and I will look at that."

Hamilton added: "It was a nightmare. Just low grip, felt like the tyres weren't working, had some damage on the floor that appeared out of nowhere and was losing 0.3-0.4secs and then had a deployment issue that lost us 0.6secs and with that we were nowhere, and I had no-one ahead of me. That wasn't great. So everything wasn't great.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/netball/arti: Captain James Thomson-Boston will lead England out to face Jamaica
It's not that men aren't playing it - it's just that you're not seeing it.
That is the message echoed by both James Thomson-Boston - captain of the England men's netball side - and Jamaica defender Authorn Chambers.
These two men's sides have history, and are about to meet again.

In a historic first, their matches will be played as curtain-raisers before England's women, ranked third in the world, face fourth-placed Jamaica in the Vitality Netball Horizon Series in London this weekend.
With an inaugural men's World Cup on the cards, likely within the next few years, BBC Sport looks at the signs that indicate that, if not already, the men's game will soon be on your radar.
A new era for England Roses under Stembridge - watch on the BBC
The narrative of women's sport fighting for recognition in a historically male-dominated space is a familiar one, but in netball - traditionally a female sport - it is quite the opposite.
Yet in recent years, the rise of the men's game has been meteoric.
The England men's team, known as the Thorns - in contrast to the women's Roses - played their first international in October 2022 and are now coached by women's Netball Super League coach Jo Noel.

They have played international Test series against the likes of Australia, toured St Kitts & Nevis for the Americas Netball Men's Championship, and are now set to play Jamaica for the first time on home soil.
Overseas, Australia and New Zealand contest the Trans-Tasman Cup, while African nations play in the Africa Netball Cup.
And now, 63 years after the first women's World Cup, the sport's global governing body, World Netball, says plans are being developed to host an inaugural men's edition.

In a statement to BBC Sport, it said: "World Netball will always remain proud of the sport's unique female-focused foundations; however we are also a sport that is open to all. We should celebrate and be proud of our traditions but not a hostage to them.
"World Netball feels that now is the right time to intentionally build men into our ecosystem and provide them with an elite platform through which to showcase their skills to the world."
For Chambers, a potential World Cup represents a huge opportunity to get even more eyes on the men's game.
"It needs to be in those kind of spaces that people are seeing it - that's how it's going to grow," he said.
"This sport deserves to have a spotlight on it, be it female or male or altogether," Thomson-Boston added. "I think we just need to keep pushing and keep shouting about it because visibility is key.
"If every men's netball game around the world was now streamed somewhere, you got a notification, you'd realise how many people are actually playing the sport day in, day out."
The England-Jamaica matches on Saturday and Sunday will be streamed on the England Men's & Mixed Netball Association (EMMNA) YouTube channel.
Thomson-Boston moved to England from Australia 10 years ago. While searching for a netball club to join, he was asked if he actually meant a football club.
Now the questions he is asked are often by mothers of young boys, keen to get their sons involved in netball.
"People always apologise in the DMs - 'I'm so sorry to do this', and I'm like, 'no, flood the DMs. Ask every question you want, because you're going to love it when you step out on court'."
Along with that, Thomson-Boston believes the perception of men playing what is, at its roots, a female-led sport, continues to change - even since the captain last spoke to BBC Sport in May 2025.
Instead of people saying "a guy playing men's netball, that seems a bit strange", he says this has now shifted to excitement and curiosity: "How do you train? How do I find out more about it?"

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/sport/2717125: The home of rugby has been a field of mixed fortune for the All Blacks.
While Twickenham has seen some of the side's greatest triumphs, it has also played host to a few of its darkest days.
This weekend could well define Dave Rennie's rookie year, after a shock loss to Wales, his side need to respond against the English at 'Twickers'.
With so much on the line in London, including a place in the first ever Nations Championship final, RNZ takes a look back at the best and worst All Black performances on the hallowed turf.

One of the All Blacks finest hours . A side packed with legends from skipper Richie McCaw, Dan Carter, Ma'a Nonu, Conrad Smith, Keven Mealamu, and Tony Woodcock, playing their final test, closing out the last true era of dominance from the men in black. After a clinical early try for Nehe Milner-Skudder, Nonu scored an individual stunner from halfway, before Carter put things out of reach with a penalty and drop goal. The final nail came as Ben Smith stabbed a kick ahead from his own 22 for Beauden Barrett to fly on to, expertly control, and ground to secure a third World Cup title. Carter capped off the victory with a cheeky right footed conversion, such was the confidence of the '15 side.

Just a week earlier, the All Blacks endured one of their most bruising ever battles with the Boks to secure their place in the final. Despite out-scoring South Africa two tries to none through Milner-Skudder and Jerome Kaino, Handre Pollard kept his side in touch with five penalties, Pat Lambie coming on to nail one of his own to reduce the margin to two. But despite the late Springbok onslaught, the All Black defence held firm, a Ben Franks hit jolting the ball free to end another famous clash between the old rivals.
Richie McCaw and Kieran Read celebrate their semi final win over South Africa.

"It's 1995 all over again," Keith Quinn roared as Jonah Lomu once again rampaged his way through the English defence on the world stage . Having sent them tumbling out of the tournament four years prior with his spectacular quartet in Cape Town, Lomu repeated the dose of damage in their own backyard, steamrolling four English on his way to a fifty metre scorcher. The All Blacks were on fire early after Christian Cullen, controversially playing centre, sliced through the line to set up Jeff Wilson. Johnny Wilkinson kept England in the hunt, but after Lomu broke the 16-all deadlock, the win was sealed when Byron Kelleher sneaked down the blindside to ensure the All Blacks would top Pool B.

The Invincibles left a lasting mark on Europe , including at Twickenham, becoming the first All Blacks side to play at the famous ground and securing the first All Blacks win. A gruelling tour off the field but a flawless one on it, the formidable side arrived at Twickenham having swept their way past 27 opponents for 27 wins, with just five matches remaining on the historic tour. The London leg included three matches at Twickenham, two county games and the third of four tests on tour. The English test is perhaps most remembered for the dramatic sending off of Cyril Brownlie, the first All Black to be given his marching orders. Brother Maurice would respond with one of four All Black tries, as they established a 14-point lead with 14 men, before a late surge from the home side made for a more respectable scoreline. The side would win their final four games on tour to return home with a perfect 32 from 32 record. The result would be the first of six wins on the trot for the All Blacks over England, a run that was finally broken in 1936.

A win over Procházka could see Stirling handed a title shot in a division desperate for new talent.

The last being against current champion and Kiwi Ulberg, who overcame a leg injury to knock out the unorthodox Czech fighter in the first round at UFC 327 in April.

New Zealand's Dan Hooker looks on after his loss to France's Benoit Saint Denis at UFC 325.

Touted as a future Silver Fern, Georgie Edgecombe is at a crucial point in her netball career.

As she works to establish herself among the country's upper echelon of players, she faces an increasingly difficult question - how do you prepare as an elite athlete, without an elite pathway or contract?

The 25-year-old is one of a group of players caught in limbo, after Netball New Zealand abandoned plans to privatise the elite domestic competition , just eight weeks after signing a non-binding term sheet with investors Anna Mowbray and Ali Williams .
The collapse of the deal blindsided players, who had already endured months of uncertainty over their professional futures.

Netball New Zealand is currently working on an alternative plan for an elite domestic competition in 2027 , but chief executive Jennah Wootten could not guarantee the players would be paid. The national body is yet to announce any details for next year and beyond.

While 18 players will head overseas next season , most to Australia's Suncorp Super Netball competition, several current Silver Ferns, including Peta Toeava, Martina Salmon, Parris Mason and Laura Balmer, remain without a contract.
For emerging players like Edgecombe, the uncertainty also threatens access to the high-performance environment they need to take the next step.

"Obviously, you've got to play and be in form to be selected, and especially with the World Cup coming up next year. It's a little bit on my mind, but there's not much we can do, except prepare the best we can, in case something does come around."

Edgecombe was named in the 2024/25 Silver Ferns development squad, which - for several years - was designed to bridge the gap between domestic netball and the Silver Ferns by building depth and giving emerging players high-performance exposure.
Retired rugby player Ali Williams and entrepreneur Anna Mowbray.
Netball New Zealand has not announced a separate development squad since that 24/25 cohort.

Typically, a Silver Ferns squad of between 16-18 players would be named each year, while up to 10 players would also be named in a development squad, which played a role in succession planning. An 18-player 2026/2027 Silver Ferns squad was named in September.

Beauden Barrett's All Blacks career has taken another remarkable turn, with the veteran playmaker on the verge of a milestone few could have imagined when he was overlooked at the start of the season .
The 35-year-old will become just the fourth player in rugby history to play 150 tests when he runs out at Twickenham on Sunday morning (NZT), having been named to start at fullback against England.
He will be the first back to reach the milestone and only the second All Black to do so. He is also just four tests away from overtaking Sam Whitelock (153) as New Zealand's most-capped player.
All Blacks coach Dave Rennie, who took charge of the team at the start of the season, said it was a remarkable achievement.
"It's a phenomenal feat for a start to bring up 150 tests," Rennie told reporters in London. "He's been a brilliant player for a long time."
Although Rennie has only worked with Barrett for a few months, the coach said the veteran's professionalism and influence had made a lasting impression.
"What I've been most impressed with is the quality of the man he is off-field as well.
"He leads really well. He deeply cares about the jersey and the legacy and is constantly driving that. He's an excellent influence on all our young men coming through the system.
"Fifteen years at this level is phenomenal and to be playing at the quality that he's played and the form that he's in speaks volumes."
Barrett has retained his place in the starting side to face England, with Rennie making eight changes following last weekend's shock loss to Wales .

Several first choice players return to the starting XV , including lock Fabian Holland, loose forward Tupou Vaa'i, hooker and captain Codie Taylor, midfielder Jordie Barrett and star wing Will Jordan, who is back from a hamstring injury earlier than expected.

Jordan, the All Blacks' leading try-scorer with 56 test tries, has seen Barrett's influence first-hand. The pair have played together throughout Jordan's international career, with the younger back crediting Barrett as one of the people who helped shape him as an All Black.
"It's been one of the great privileges of my All Black career, playing with Beaudy and being around him as a team-mate," Jordan said.
"Someone I class as good friend, he was certainly someone who took me under their wing when I first came into the team and he's done that with every player."
Jordan, who will bring up his 65th test on the weekend, said Barrett's longevity was difficult to comprehend.
"One hundred and fifty tests is a crazy feat of longevity," Jordan said.
"I was a reflecting yesterday and it feels like I've been around for a while now and I'm at 65 tests this weekend, so I'm only halfway.
"I've got Damian McKenzie or Jordie Barrett's full test career to go to get to Beaudy's achievement, which seems ridiculous."
Beauden Barrett (centre) looks dejected following the loss to Wales.
Barrett's path to the milestone has not been straightforward.
He was overlooked for the All Blacks' first six tests of the year, with Rennie making it clear the veteran had slipped down the pecking order.
But he has fought his way back into the starting side, starting New Zealand's last four tests and putting himself within touching distance of Whitelock's all-time record.
Jordan said Barrett's achievement was a reflection of his relentless work ethic, and the All Blacks were determined to mark the occasion with a win.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crje: In two years, Westside Cowboy have rocketed from the sweaty corners of Manchester's student pub circuit to performances on one of America's biggest talk shows and at many of the UK's biggest festivals.

A typical cold winter night on Oldham Street, Manchester, where four students are set to play their first headline show together in the innocuous backroom of a little pub called The Castle Hotel.
Wolstenholme, pictured with Murphy and Bradbury, has championed the band since the start

I played it on BBC Introducing on BBC Radio Lancashire that very night, and quickly forwarded it to the BBC Introducing Mixtape.
Westside Cowboy had the attention of the nation's music media.

Westside Cowboy formed in 2023, having played together in other bands

Sessions where the modus operandi was shaking off the pretensions of their other perhaps more lofty-minded projects, and taking things back to basics to rediscover the answer to the question of why they actually loved playing music - because it was fun.
Within a few short months they were one of the country's hottest underground prospects, with videos of their live shows spreading all over Instagram.
Westside Cowboy were one of four local artists showcased by BBC Introducing at The Grand in Clitheroe.
It was a set laden with songs they would release in the subsequent 18 months.
Then in April, I was calling them from our radio studio to tell them that they had been awarded one of the coveted spots on the BBC Introducing stage at Glastonbury Festival 2025.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c615: Morfydd Clark plays the elf Galadriel, portrayed by Cate Blanchett in Peter Jackson's Lord of the Rings film trilogy
Actress Morfydd Clark has described how filming The Rings of Power allowed her to see "all these secret bits" of Wales she had not visited before.
The fantasy adventure is set thousands of years before the events of JRR Tolkien's The Hobbit and Lord of the Rings in the fictional Middle Earth.
Clark, who is from Penarth, Vale of Glamorgan, was able to see parts of her own country she had not explored before while filming the third series of the Amazon Prime Video programme.
The star is reprising her leading role as the fierce elf commander Galadriel - and has also admitted how she slipped some Welsh words into her role.
Clark said her mother used to wait for the credits to see the interesting places where programmes had been shot.
It is reported The Rings of Power was filmed at Neath Abbey and Trefil Quarry, Blaenau Gwent, among other places.
Last autumn, the cast was also spotted in Devon , shooting along the coast.
"Look at the credits," Clark said, urging fans to do the same as her mum to find out where it was filmed.
It is not only the scenery that may be familiar to people from Wales, but Tolkien's invented Elvish language has been described as having Celtic influences .
Clark, a fluent Welsh speaker, admitted slipping some words in, including the command "cer" to her horse – the Welsh word for "go".
During series one, Galadriel was seen shouting the command "cer" to her horse, the Welsh word for "go"
The actress, who has also starred in Dracula and His Dark Materials, warned fans that all is not well for the protagonists in the upcoming series, joking: "It's going terribly."
Referring to the evil sorcerer who is trying to take over the fictional Middle Earth, Clark said: "Sauron is back and powerful and evil.
Series three is set five years after the events of series two, and hope is dim in Middle Earth as Sauron's armies have conquered almost all in their path.
A few pockets of resistance remain, including Galadriel and her fellow elves, but Sauron works day and night to harness the power of the One Ring to crush them.
In the series, the "sorcerer of dreadful power" Sauron is played by Charlie Vickers, who starred in Netflix historical drama Medici
Despite this, Clark says the series will also look back on Galadriel's happier days, where the audience will see the serious commander dance and be cheerful.
Clark enjoyed the chance to "go back in time" and explore this new side of her character, adding: "It felt really exciting to go and find a different part of who she was."
In Jackson's Lord of the Rings film trilogy, Galadriel is serene and wise yet immensely powerful.
Meanwhile, the Prime Video prequel depicts the character in her youth, wilful and rebellious.
"It's wonderful to play someone brave and unapologetic, and also not afraid of social consequences," Clark said.
"I like to try and push myself to be a bit more like her at times."
Clark is joined in series three by Stranger Things actor Jamie Campbell Bower, who plays Galadriel's long-lost husband Celeborn
The Lord of the Rings franchise is globally beloved, so taking on such a recognised role as Galadriel comes with a lot of pressure, believes Clark.
However, given that an actor's job is to "make a career out of emotions", she feels a similar responsibility in all her acting pursuits.
"I've just resigned myself to the fact the neurosis will always be there, whether I'm doing a speech at Christmas or filming this," she said.
Series three of Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is available to watch now.

The film's director, Guillaume Nicloux, has been accused of being complicit because he was said to have filmed the incident, Mediapart and AFP report. The BBC has contacted his agent and the Paris prosecutor's office for comment.
Nicloux told Mediapart that the scene had been improvised and he had not intervened as he had not observed "any constraints, verbal or physical opposition, or even discomfort".
The site published production documents showing footage of the scene had been destroyed.

The actress told the outlet that she had told friends, her agent and others involved in the film's production in Normandy about the incident at the time, but only filed the complaint after other women accused Depardieu of sexual misconduct.
The Asterix and Obelix star will next week find out whether he will stand trial for allegedly raping another actress, Charlotte Arnould.
On Monday, Depardieu dropped his appeal against a separate conviction for two counts of sexual assault during another film shoot, for which he was handed an 18-month suspended sentence.
Several other women have made allegations against the 77-year-old in the media.
