https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8xg: Switching to heat pumps is seen as a key way to help meet the UK's net zero targets
Developers will have to install heat pumps and solar panels in all new homes in England under regulations announced in March .
The changes are estimated to add £10,000 to the price of new homes, though owners will likely save money on energy bills over the long term.
In January, the government introduced a £15bn Warm Homes Plan to help UK households pay for green technologies as part of efforts to reduce fossil fuel use and energy bills.
But the autumn budget cut £1bn from the programme to pay for defence.
Heating homes accounts for about a fifth of the UK's planet-warming emissions, so switching from gas and oil to heat pumps is seen as a key way to help meet net zero targets .
Heat pumps run on electricity instead of gas and are more efficient than traditional boilers. They warm buildings by absorbing and amplifying heat from the air, ground or water.

Air source heat pumps - the most common type - suck in outdoor air and pass it over tubes containing refrigerant fluids. The heat from the outdoor air causes the refrigerants to evaporate into a gas. Compressing the gas increases the temperature, and this heat is passed around the home.
The system consists of a box measuring about 1m x 1m x 0.4m (3ft x 3ft x 1.3ft) which stands outside the property, as well as a heat pump unit and hot water cylinder inside the property.
The indoor unit is about the size of a gas boiler, while the size of the cylinder depends on the property.
Ground source heat pumps are more efficient than air source models.
However, they are typically more expensive and less commonly used, as they require either a deep bore hole or a large horizontal system dug into the ground.
The Boiler Upgrade Scheme provides a grant of £7,500 towards the cost of an air source or ground source heat pump for homeowners in England and Wales.
Households typically spend an additional £5,000 on top of the grant, which the UK's spending watchdog warned is too high for many .

The grant can be used for existing homes and non-domestic buildings. The property must have an eligible Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) - a measure of how your property is performing - issued in the last 10 years.
Properties no longer need to have existing loft or cavity wall insulation to qualify for the grant, which can save around £2,500 in upfront costs.
Check if you are eligible for the Boiler Upgrade Scheme , external
For low-income households and those in social housing, the government is providing an extra £5bn for the Warm Homes Local Grant , external and the Social Housing Fund , external .
Scotland , external and Northern Ireland , external have separate schemes to help make homes more efficient.
UK households can also apply for low and no interest loans of between £7,500 and £35,000 to install green technologies under the Warm Homes Loan Scheme , external .
The government has promised to keep funding for the Boiler Upgrade Scheme at £400m in 2027-28 before increasing it in line with inflation.
However, this represents a significant cut compared to what was previously announced.

Some of the money the energy and environment departments have to spend on loans and investments is also being diverted towards the £4.7bn "Your First Home" scheme, which aims to help people purchase a property.
This could mean further cuts to the Warm Homes Scheme, but the government has said it "remains committed to heat-pump deployment".
Heat pump installations currently benefit from a 0% VAT rate, but this is set to rise to 5% in April 2027.

While the upfront costs remain substantial, heat pumps could become cheaper to run than gas boilers, according to the Climate Change Committee (CCC) , external , which advises the UK government on cutting emissions.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c39w: After an eight-year journey travelling almost six billion miles (10bn km), a spacecraft called BepiColombo is about to reach its final destination and get into orbit around Mercury.

It will be entering an extremely hostile environment: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and temperatures can reach a fierce 430C and then plunge to -180C, and it is constantly blasted with intense solar radiation.
Until now, the planet has been little explored but the hope is this mission will solve some of Mercury's major mysteries.
These include uncovering why there is ice in its craters despite its proximity to the Sun, and understanding the mysterious hollows that are dotted all over its surface.

"I think it's a little bit of an under-loved planet in the inner Solar System, but I think that's one of the reasons why it is so compelling," said Prof Emma Bunce, from Leicester University, who is a principal investigator on the mission.

"There are lots of reasons, scientifically, why we really want to understand Mercury, how it formed, how it evolved, what it looks like today, but also how it interacts with the Sun and the extreme space weather that it experiences."
The spacecraft - just seen here - has taken selfies as it has closed in on Mercury
The BepiColombo mission, which is a collaboration between the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japanese Space Agency (JAXA), blasted off in 2018 , launching from French Guiana.
With the spacecraft heading deep into the inner Solar System, it has had to battle the Sun's immense gravitational pull.

So it has had its brakes on for the entire journey, and has also taken a very convoluted path - looping once around the Earth, twice around Venus and six times around Mercury - to slow it down enough to get into orbit.
This journey should have taken seven years, but a problem with BepiColombo's propulsion system meant the already epic voyage was extended by a year.
The final manoeuvre to get into orbit is a perilous one: it needs to perform a 37-minute handbrake turn to be grabbed by the planet's gravity.
If anything goes wrong, the spacecraft could hurtle past Mercury.
Only two spacecraft have visited Mercury until now - both Nasa missions.
Mariner-10 flew past the planet three times in the 1970s, and then the Messenger spacecraft arrived at Mercury in 2011 and spent four years in orbit.
Mercury is only a bit bigger than our Moon, and is covered in ancient volcanoes, towering cliffs and colossal craters.
The planet zips around the Sun so quickly, a year on Mercury lasts just 88 Earth days. But it turns incredibly slowly on its own axis, so a single day there lasts 59 Earth days.
These strange hollows have not been seen anywhere else in the Universe
As well as investigating why Mercury has ice in its craters in the polar regions, the mission will also spend time studying strange dents in the planet's surface.
There are thousands of hollows all over it. They are shallow but with steep sides and often clustered together, and in planetary terms, they are young: about 100,000 years old.
Scientists know they are not impact craters - larger pockmarks on the surface caused by colliding space rocks - but they are not really sure what the hollows are or how they formed.
BepiColombo will also help to study another aspect of Mercury that has been puzzling researchers. Despite the planet's tiny size, it has a huge metal core.
Prof Emma Bunce said that the planet could once have been much bigger, but was potentially the victim of a "hit and run" early in its history.
"One of the explanations is that the mantle was stripped away in a large collision," she explained.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c607: Africa is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (£30bn)
In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day.
A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable.
"Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC.
"Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up."
Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed.
Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding.
In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district.
Nkhambala fled to higher ground with his wife and four children as floodwaters swept through his village.
"As we reached a safe height, we saw our house swept away right in front of our eyes. Everything I had was gone," he told the BBC.
He lost a harvest of 15 bags of sorghum and part of his farmland. His children were so traumatised that they stopped going to school.
"They refused to go to school for many months. They were so disturbed," he recalled.
After relocating and trying to rebuild his life, Nkhambala is now facing another climate challenge - this time a lack of rain.
"This time we fear there may be no harvest. I have no clue what I will do."
A government assessment after Cyclone Freddy found that Malawi had experienced more than 50 disasters linked to storms, floods, landslides and droughts since 1980, affecting millions of people.

While Uganda and Malawi are suffering the effects of climate change and their governments are asking for assistance adapting to the new global weather patterns, they are among 23 African countries yet to submit National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) to the UN climate convention secretariat.

These are the plans that detail how climate change has affected them and the risks they face, and so help make a case for what assistance they need. Without them, experts say, it becomes difficult to secure funding.

"Our region has experienced cyclical droughts for decades, but there has been no action plan to tackle these climate impacts," said Milton Lorpia, who works for Warrior Squad Foundation in Karamoja region of Uganda.
"If only such a plan were in place and implemented, it would certainly have helped us."
Mathews Nkhambala and his wife fear their harvest may fail this year

The African Group of Negotiators at the ongoing UN climate summit (COP31) in Turkey is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (£30bn) baseline that it says developed countries committed to providing by 2025. The interpretation of that commitment remains contested.
The proposal was not accepted for formal negotiations at the summit, although African negotiators have continued to push for it.
The funding is intended to help vulnerable countries prepare for and withstand climate change-induced extreme weather, such as droughts, floods and wildfires.
But the European Union, one of the largest providers of climate finance, says the priority should be ensuring existing commitments reach vulnerable countries rather than setting new funding targets.

"We haven't come to the table with additional monies or additional capital. It's about what we have committed already and ensuring it's deployed," Darragh O'Brien, who leads the EU delegation at COP31 on behalf of the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, told a press conference.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6qj: A bar-tailed godwit similar to Phil being fitted with a tracking device
A bird named Phil has astonished conservationists by completing a 6,800-mile (10,900km) round trip from England's east coast to Siberia and back.
Bar-tailed godwits are champion fliers, migrating between Britain and the Arctic, but the precise routes used by individual birds is largely unknown.
Phil was fitted with a tiny solar-powered tracker that recorded his movements throughout the journey.
The data showed he travelled from The Wash , external to the Wadden Sea, along the coasts of the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark, before continuing to Siberia.
On his return, he crossed the Arctic Ocean to northern Norway, stopping on three islands before heading back through the Wadden Sea to The Wash.
Scientists say Phil's extraordinary travels highlight the importance of protecting the world's wetlands, which are havens for millions of migratory birds each year.

Dr Nigel Clark, of the conservation charity, The Wash Wader Research Group, said The Wash is the UK's single most important coastal wetland for migratory waders, with spectacular numbers seen in autumn and winter.
"Tracking birds like Phil the Godwit shows us how connected the Wash is with the rest of the flyway," he said.
Jeff Kew, RSPB Coastal Advisor, said many migratory bird species cross borders, depending on a whole network of wetlands along the way.
That's why it's so important to look after these special places."
Bar-tailed godwits are wading birds of similar size to pigeons, but with long bills and legs.

They are regarded as one of nature's long-distance endurance athletes, with one subspecies making the longest known non-stop migration of any bird, flying 8,425 miles (13,559km) from Alaska to New Zealand.
Phil's journey included a handful of stops to rest and refuel.
He will now spend the winter relaxing with thousands of other wading birds at the Snettisham Nature Reserve in Norfolk.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c920: Bududa has suffered repeated deadly landslides over the years
Survivors of a 2019 landslide in eastern Uganda that killed more than 50 people have taken their fight for relocation and compensation to the United Nations.
The 48 complainants accuse the government of violating Uganda's constitution by failing to put effective disaster management measures in Bududa, a mountainous district prone to landslides.
Their case comes as heavy rains raise the risk of further landslides. They say the government relocation programme ignores their safety, land rights and livelihoods.
The UN Human Rights Committee is considering what is believed to be the first case seeking climate adaptation measures, one that could set a global precedent.
At least 33 of the 53 people who died in the 2019 landslide were children. Years later, survivors say every spell of heavy rain brings back fears of another tragedy.
William Tsama, one of the claimants, lost four members of his family.
"Victims in such situations, ignored by governments, can take them to court to compel them to help their citizens."
Uganda introduced a resettlement plan for landslide-prone areas in 2011, but progress has been limited, with relatively few people relocated.
Last month, it launched a new resettlement programme offering affected households 18m Ugandan shillings ($4,300; £3,300) to help them move to safer areas.
But some survivors have questioned whether the amount is enough to cover the cost of relocating and rebuilding their lives.

Under the programme, families can choose between receiving two acres of land, valued at 8m shillings, plus 10m shillings towards building a house, or taking the equivalent land allowance in cash, alongside the same housing grant.
The scheme is expected to benefit 1,410 households identified as living in high-risk areas.
The government has now given residents of designated high-risk areas two months, from November to December, to leave or face forced eviction.

The threat extends beyond landslides. The complainants say changing rainfall patterns and declining soil fertility have also affected farming, leaving many families struggling to secure their livelihoods.
"I want to get a new good place for my people, so even if I die, they will be okay. I am an old man, but I am doing it for my children," Tsama said.
The survivors first launched legal action in 2020 in Uganda, and received support from Ugandan environmental organisation Greenwatch three years later.
They are seeking compensation for lost family members and livelihoods, as well as emergency measures, including accessible early-warning systems in high-risk areas.
Greenwatch Executive Director Samantha Atukunda Kakuru Mwesigwa said the case is about changing how governments prepare and respond to climate-related disasters.

"Justice for claimants is not just about winning in court. It is about forcing government policy to keep pace with a changing climate, and ensuring loss and damage is no longer an afterthought in disaster management," she said.
The threat of climate-related disasters extends across East Africa.
In Kenya, floods and landslides killed at least 181 people between March and May 2024, according to the Kenya Red Cross. In Rwanda, floods and landslides killed 135 people in May 2023.

The dangers are also being felt further afield. In October 2026, a flash flood swept through Nepal's Gorkha district after a landslide blocked a river, washing away homes and infrastructure, and killing over 1,500 people.

"Disasters like the one in Bududa are only getting worse because of climate change – and they are happening all around the world, as we've seen recently and tragically in Nepal," ClientEarth lawyer Vesselina Newman said.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmd7: Brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei are chief executive and president of Anthropic
In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.
The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.
Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at $83 each, it said on Wednesday.
At that price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $19.3bn (£14.7bn) each.
So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?
In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.
He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track , and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.
Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.
Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.
But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.
Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".
Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.
She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.
Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.
She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.
The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.
Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.
He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.
Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.
He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".
Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.
Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.

Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.
He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.
Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8p3: Special Protection Areas are home to rare and threatened birds like the curlew
An investigation has found the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs is failing to protect wild birds.
The Office for Environmental Protection said Daera had not complied with environmental law requiring it to classify and update Special Protection Areas (SPAs).
Environment Minister Andrew Muir said their findings made for "uncomfortable reading".
SPAs are home to rare and threatened birds like the curlew and whooper swan, which continue to decline in Northern Ireland.
The OEP said action had not been taken to maintain or restore wild bird populations and their habitats.
The director of RSPB NI, Joanne Sherwood, said the findings were "no surprise" and called for urgent action.
A parallel investigation is looking at the same issues involving Defra and Natural England, and they have also been issued with decision notices.

In Northern Ireland, the OEP's Chief Regulatory Officer Helen Venn acknowledged that "positive steps" had been taken, but added that delays in meeting legal obligations had played a part in the significant decline of wild birds in Northern Ireland.

"SPAs are important for achieving the Executive's commitments in relation to nature, such as the strategic outcome of thriving, resilient and connected nature and wildlife in the Environmental Improvement Plan.
"This is in addition to the Executive's international commitment to protect at least 30% of land and seas for nature's recovery by 2030.

"This is why it is important for Daera to carry out its legal responsibilities in a reasonable timeframe to deliver nature recovery and in relation to the classification and adaptation of SPAs on land."
The agriculture and environment minister Andrew Muir said there was "a moral and legal obligation" to protect wild bird habitats and welcomed continuing engagement between his officials and the OEP.

"The OEP has recognised in their investigation longstanding and concerning failures to implement recommended actions to protect wild bird habitats and populations by successive administrations both in England and Northern Ireland.
"While we have a long way to go to reverse current trends, there are signs of hope and clear examples of nature recovery in action.
"However, the scale of challenge requires greater levels of support from across government to provide the necessary resources and funding to address the nature crisis."
And he said the recently-published Nature Recovery Strategy and the Farming With Nature support package "reinforces" the department's commitment to nature restoration.
Sherwood said the group had been highlighting failing for decades.
"Today's findings from the OEP confirm what conservation organisations have been saying: action has been delayed for far too long.

"The focus must now move to delivery, with the Executive leading the way, and Daera and NIEA being resourced to take urgent action to put these protections in place and help reverse the decline of our most vulnerable bird populations.
The decision notice is the latest step in the OEP's investigation.
It identifies failures and recommends what actions Daera should now take to fix them.
It says Daera has failed to classify and update SPAs, has not put measures in place to protect declining birds, and has not carried out a required review of habitats.
Recommendations include addressing outstanding recommendations "where they remain ecologically relevant" from a review of SPAs, carried out in Northern Ireland in 2001.
Where they cannot be implemented, it says "transparent, ornithological reasons" must be published.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm62: Firefighter Steve Williams, pictured here with his widow Jilska, died of a rare lung cancer 14 years after falling into a toxic lagoon
It was a sight which struck terror into the firefighters called to tackle it - a blazing chemical waste lagoon on fire, with barrels exploding into the air.
Steve Williams, then in his 20s, was one of 60 firefighters sent to tackle the burning Llwyneinion lagoon in August 1980, which was sending thick black smoke over a nearby village.
Steve slipped in and, although he was pulled out, his widow thinks what he swallowed may have cost him his life from a rare form of lung cancer aged 39. She said "someone should be held accountable".
Wrexham council, which owns the site, said while it did not meet the legal definition of "contaminated land", it regularly inspected and monitored the area.
It took 60 firefighters about 18 hours to bring the 1980 fire at Llwyneinion lagoon under control
A leading expert in fire chemistry and toxicity said it was difficult to establish a link between firefighters' exposure to chemicals and health issues later in life.
Steve's widow Jilska Williams believes the father-of-two's terminal cancer could have stemmed from the chemicals at the fire at the former toxic waste dump near Wrexham in north Wales.

"It's a definite probability," said the 71-year-old. "They're firemen and they're always running into fires, so you don't know what the long-term effects are going to be - but actually falling into the lake and drinking that fluid, which is full of chemicals. He had a double-whammy, didn't he?"
Steve's family are part of a group which came forward after the BBC documentary Buried with Michael Sheen highlighted Wales' toxic waste legacy.
This is the last family photo of Jilska and Steve Williams, with their children David and Kelly, taken in June 1994, shortly before he was diagnosed with terminal lung cancer
They want surviving firefighters to be tested for deadly carcinogens they fear they were exposed to in the fire at the Llwyneinion lagoon.
Eleven firefighters or their families have told a BBC investigation about concerns the fire could have had an impact on their health.
They said there was an increased number of miscarriages suffered by partners of those who attended the fire in the year after - and also highlighted concerns about rates of cancers since.
Steve followed his dad into the fire service in 1978 and his first posting was in Wrexham, where he was among the first responders to the lagoon fire.
The 1980 fire at a lagoon used as a dumping site for chemicals was fought for two days.
Jilska said he was checked at hospital after falling in, then given a tetanus injection before being sent home.
"What is a tetanus injection going to do for him?" said the retired nurse. "It was a disaster waiting to happen. A time bomb waiting to go off, as far as I'm concerned."
The couple moved to Melbourne in Australia, then in 1994 Steve was diagnosed with stage four cancer - small cell carcinoma , external - and given weeks to live.
Footage from a BBC news report in August 1980 shows the extent of the toxic waste dump fire at the Llwyneinion lagoon
He died three days after the couple's 17th wedding anniversary. Their children were aged six and 10.
The Llwyneinion site was a dumping ground for chemicals suspected to have included cancer-causing polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) from chemical giant Monsanto.

Sheen's Buried programme team found elevated levels of PCBs in soil samples taken in an area open to the public beyond the fenced-off lagoon, as well as at 13 other suspected dumpsites for the firm's toxic waste across the country.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm75: The official sign on the banks of the River Tone at French Weir Park in Taunton advises people not to swim.
But that hasn't stopped Jo, Jenny, Sue and a second Jo from enjoying a regular dip together.

"People think, oh you're swimming down by the supermarket, that can't be very nice, but it's gorgeous," Jenny Hillier says, as the women huddle round with their coats and hot drinks after a bracing October plunge.
People have been swimming at the spot on the River Tone in the centre of Taunton for more than a hundred years.
But it is only since 2024 that French Weir Park has been designated an official bathing site, which means from May to September the water gets tested by the Environment Agency (EA).
Those tests regularly confirm what the women's senses have been telling them for a while - the water quality is poor.

"There are times when we've come down and we haven't got in, either because of the look or the smell," says Jo Macdonald. "We don't take risks. We don't put our faces in. We don't swim with cuts or anything."
"This summer I got quite poorly," Jenny says, explaining that she'd had diarrhoea, vomiting and muscle cramps.
"I'd swum and then within six hours I was unwell. I was poorly for probably about seven to 10 days and it was not nice. I think it was the river that day."
"There are germs everywhere, all over the place. You can catch Covid in Tesco," she says.
The BBC has been investigating whether discharges of treated sewage might be responsible for poor water quality at a bathing site in Taunton.

This summer French Weir Park failed its tests on 13 of the 19 days it was sampled. The BBC analysed data from all four regulators across the UK for 2026 and found French Weir Park's failure rate of 68% was the highest of all the bathing sites.
The regulators look for two types of faecal bacteria – E. coli and intestinal enterococci – that originate either in human or animal guts and can make people ill if ingested.
So where's it coming from at French Weir Park? The local water company Wessex Water says it could have come from wildlife, agriculture, private septic tanks as well as its sewerage works.
We decided to take a closer look to see if we could work out where the truth lies.
Despite the high levels of faecal bacteria and the health warnings, Jenny, Jo and Jo have kept swimming at the bathing site in Taunton
Our wastewater treatment system is built on the assumption that faecal bacteria - from our poo - once discharged into nature will be rapidly diluted and perish.
The bacteria are known to have little impact on wildlife but they can make humans sick if ingested – so the rise in popularity of wild-swimming and testing of bathing sites have increased awareness.
As part of a BBC investigation we analysed the water sampling results from this summer across all the UK's 700 official bathing sites on the coast, in lakes and rivers.
We found that more than 10% of the UK's coastal sites and 37% of its inland sites failed to meet regulators' minimum standards across the summer.
That difference is likely to be because the sea acts as a more effective dispersant and can dilute and kill faecal bacteria quicker than a lake or river.
Of the 11 worst bathing sites in England in 2026, seven were on inland rivers or lakes.
Last year the official advice was not to swim at 12 of the 14 inland river bathing sites in England .

Poor water quality has historically been linked to raw sewage spills. These are much more likely after it has rained. So why, in a summer that was extremely dry, did bacteria levels remain high in so many rivers?
In Taunton the official testing data suggests there has been a constant flow of bacteria entering the river.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c63r: The UK is likely to miss legally binding climate targets if the government reduces electric vehicle (EV) targets, independent adviser the Climate Change Committee (CCC) has warned.

In a letter to Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander, the CCC argues that weakening the targets would result in "economic and energy security costs" and leave households "more exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices".
The CCC says that switching to an electric vehicle can save a typical household around £800 a year, with fewer people benefiting if the targets were watered down.
The warning comes after weeks of speculation that the government plans to announce changes to the EV targets. Government sources insist no decision has been made.

Under the current rules, a "zero emission vehicle" (ZEV) mandate requires 80% of new cars sold in the UK to be zero emission by 2030 and all new cars to meet that standard by 2035. Companies that fail to meet their ZEV mandate face a potential fine of £12,000 per car, although there are exemptions.
Industry groups have long complained the current rules impose too heavy a burden, calling instead for a "sustainable transition".
Latest data from trade body the Society of Motor Manufacturing and Traders (SMMT) shows that EVs, as well as plug-in hybrids, are driving growth in new car sales.
In the year so far, 26.6% of all new car registrations have been fully electric, the SMMT says, which is below the headline target of 33% for 2026.

But the industry as a whole appears on course to comply with this year's mandate once flexibilities are accounted for, according to analysis by New AutoMotive, a transport research organisation which supports the transition to electric cars
SMMT Chief Executive Mike Hawes accused the CCC of ignoring the costs of the targets it was defending.
"The industry cannot subsidise the transition indefinitely, which is why it is unified in seeking change," he said.
The CCC analysis also argued that weakening the targets would lead to a hole in the government's carbon savings that need to be made in order to meet its legally binding climate targets.

The CCC said the ZEV mandate "underpins the largest share of emissions reduction to 2037" in the government's net-zero plan. The climate targets set for 2033-2037 will be missed "without alternative action at the same scale", the CCC argued.
CCC analysis shows surface transport - which includes cars, vans and trucks - remains the country's highest carbon-emitting sector and one of the slowest to decarbonise.
Lord Deben, former CCC chairman, said going against CCC advice would "not be sensible" as it would "cost people money".
He said climate targets were "not random targets" and "if you don't reach them then you put yourselves in really serious danger of having climate change, which we can't handle".

A government spokesperson said: "We remain committed to the phase out of all new petrol and diesel cars by 2030 and to all new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, as well as to our legally binding net zero targets. Our consultation on the Mandate will not change this and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmx2: The project aims to create and restore habitats for amphibians and lizards
Ponds are to be restored and freshwater habitats created for amphibians and reptiles at two former colliery sites in South Yorkshire.
The Froglife charity has been awarded nearly £890,000 of Lottery cash to carry out the work in Rother Valley, as well as at sites in North and West Yorkshire.
Kiveton and Dinnington Community Woodlands were originally regenerated through the National Coalfields Programme after the pits there closed in the 1990s.

Sheila Grundry, from Froglife, said staff were "delighted" to work in the area because "freshwater will make a lasting difference for frogs and other wildlife and it's a great way for local people to learn new skills".
The £889,761 investment in Froglife's Coalface to Wildspace project will also help local communities connect with nature, according to the charity.
Dinnington Woodland is one of the sites in Yorkshire which will be a focus of the project
The aim of the project across Yorkshire is to create 48 new ponds, improve 93 existing freshwater habitats and establish new "neighbourhood wildlife corridors" like small ponds and bug hotels.

These "corridors" will act as stepping stones for local wildlife from insects to birds, providing food, shelter and water to improve biodiversity across former industrial sites and help wildlife move between one habitat and another.
Conservationist Andy Goff, project manager in Yorkshire, said the transformation of the sites would be for everyone.
"We want people to engage with the nature that is on their doorstep and wildlife in general," he explained.
"I'm really excited about getting people involved from all over Yorkshire."
The Coalface to Wildspace project is funded by The National Lottery Heritage Fund for the next four years, with Froglife having already run similar projects in the Midlands and Scotland.
Rother Valley MP Jake Richards said the project was important for the area.
"These former industrial sites are an important part of our area's history," he said.
"This project will help transform them into thriving habitats while creating opportunities for local people to get involved."

Fire and Emergency says access to two hydrants near the site of a major central Auckland fire were blocked by a footpath and bus lane constructed over top.
On Friday morning, fire crews were called to a blaze in the ClearPoint building, a seven-storey building on Fanshawe Street.
Auckland City senior station officer Darren Gussey said there were no issues accessing the first hydrant and starting the internal fire attack.
He said the issues arose when they considered deploying an aerial appliance, which required more water.
"The first hydrant on the Fanshawe Street side we were using was covered by a footpath, and across the road, the hydrant appeared to be covered by tarseal and a bus lane," Gussey said.

"Although it didn't cause any major problems in terms of creating a risk of losing the building, there was a delay in getting water to that aerial appliance, which caused an issue, because we had to shut Fanshawe Street, which is an extremely busy road."
He said the firecrew was able to break through the tarseal to get to one of the hydrants.
Gussey said they occasionally encountered inaccessible fire hydrants, but having one covered by a complete footpath was unusual.
The Fanshawe Street fire had been particularly complex and dangerous, Gussey said.
"Where the seat of the fire was, we experienced temperatures between 600-800C and there were high-voltage electrical cables involved in the fire, so extremely dangerous to the firefighters."

"We made an initial entry into the carpark area, because my first priority is risk to life and, being a carpark, there is always a chance someone is in there. We had to send crews in there early on to conduct an initial search to ensure there was no-one in the basement of the carpark.
"Those firefighters reported to me extreme heat conditions. Once I started hearing explosions, I had to make a tactical decision to withdraw the crew for everyone's safety."

The National Cyber Security Centre is warning businesses and organisations to take steps against the rising risk of cyber attackers using AI tools.

Over the past week, there's been a rise in attackers using open source AI tool Artex to target organisations worldwide, National Cyber Security Centre cyber defence operations director Dr Emma Bickerstaffe said.
Artex was developed by researchers to check for system vulnerabilities that hackers could take advantage of.
Although it had been taken down from the internet, it had been replicated and cyber attackers were now using it to automate attacks on different organisations simultaneously, she said.
The key change was that phases of an attack could now be automated, enabling "threat actors to act faster".
"You can go from what might have previously taken weeks to a matter of hours to be able to go from initial reconnaissance, and targeting and scanning of an organisation to exploitation."
Having access to open source AI tools meant attackers could act opportunistically and were looking for any target they could gain access to, Bickerstaffe said.
"If attackers get in using AI, they can move across a system and get into an organisation's crown jewels, access data, and mess with data and change it."

She said there had been instances in New Zealand where cyber attackers had used the tool to try to get into an organisation and failed, and other incidents where they had successfully gained access to an organisation and viewed data.

Bickerstaffe advised organisations to limit the devices and systems they had connected to the internet, and implement multi-factor authentication, which could stop an attack, if a system was compromised.
Bickerstaffe's comments come after Forest & Bird and the New Zealand Defence Force both reported cyber security incidents on Friday. The tools used by the hackers are not yet known.
Forest & Bird confirmed supporters' details had been exposed .
Chief executive Sam Rowland told RNZ it had taken immediate steps to secure its systems, including a forensic search of the website that uncovered malicious files.
"We're working with our technology and cyber security experts to establish the full extent of the incident," Rowland said.
"We are contacting people we know who have been affected, explaining what information has been accessed and directing them to Own Your Online for guidance on staying safe.
"We have also notified NZ Police, the National Cyber Security Centre and the Office of the Privacy Commissioner."

Those affected and emailed were warned the stolen data could be used to create scam emails, phone calls or convincing text messages, and they should be cautious about unexpected messages, even if they contained personalised information.
The New Zealand Defence Force took some of its websites down following a breach.
NZDF was informed by its website provider of unauthorised access to its website systems.
Preliminary inquiries indicated a database associated with the Force4Families Defence Discounts scheme had been accessed, an NZDF spokesperson told RNZ.
The database included names and email addresses of registered users. Those who may have been affected have been contacted, NZDF said.
"Individuals registered through the website should remain alert to phishing emails, scams and unsolicited requests for personal information."

Hawke's Bay Assistant District Commander Hamish Smith, from the Rissington Volunteer Fire Brigade, said the community was caught out quite badly when the extreme weather struck.

AI has allowed cyber criminals to identify system vulnerabilities far more quickly than in the past.
Nicole Quinn is a vice president of global cyber security firm Palo Alto, which provides firewalls and internet security to 70,000 organisations in more than 150 countries.
She was in New Zealand last week, having earlier given evidence to an Australian Parliamentary inquiry into AI.
Quinn told Nine to Noon where a human hacker might take nine days to successfully infiltrate a system, an autonomous AI agent can do it in as little as 15 minutes.
"We have seen a significant step change in the ability of AI in the cyber security space to move fast and at scale."
She said they were not seeing new ways of undertaking cyber attacks but the change was the speed at which they could be carried out.

For example, she said a vulnerability in a phone which had not been updated previously might be spotted by criminals wanting to take advantage of it in seven to nine days but it was now taking them about 22 minutes to spot that vulnerability.
"So it's the ability for AI to quickly identify that vulnerability in organisations."
"So the scale of that speed, a machine doesn't get tired, a machine can do masses and Frontier AI the unique thing about that is can deal with such large amounts of information so quickly."
Cyber security firms would give every vulnerability a rating from 1-10 and in the past they would focus on the big vulnerabilities to close the door, she said.
"What AI, some of these frontier models can do, is to link the little ones into what then we call a significant vulnerability."
But the principles remained the same and it should be secure AI by design, she said.
It was no longer possible for businesses to rely on a once a year cyber security audit and in the world of AI continual checking was needed, she said.
She said security firms used "AI to fight AI" as the machine was needed to keep up with the machine.
"We have led that discussion on what we call machine on machine, you know the Five Eyes guidance is the speed and scale of AI, you can't do it manually so you do need AI to fight AI."
But there were also points where security firms would advise that a human needed to check what was going on, she said.
Businesses looking at introducing AI into their system needed to do so safely, she said.

"It's making sure that like any software that you bring into the organisation, you're giving it permission, you understand where it's come from, so you understand how it's been designed and then you're monitoring it into your system, just like you monitor me moving through any computer system now."
The business should also be able to retract its permissions or turn it off if behaviour changes are noticed, she said.
AI was a game changer that governments around the world were responding to, she said.

"We are not as ready as we should be and I would be setting the wrong perception if I said we had this because this is technology that we have not seen before and from a regulatory point of view, from a policy point of view, we're still flying and building the plane at the same time."
In terms of AI going rogue, in some of the high profile cases, the AI agents "leave what we thought were their guard-rails or their perimeters", she said.

The problem has been growing since the New Year period of 2021, when 56 vehicles were seen at the end of Arawhata Road. By New Year 2022 the fleet had grown to 76 vehicles.

"Thirty people so that's 300 pāua. That's just one bus to say nothing of 70 other cars down here.
"They stay here for a weekend and they come down sometimes twice a day on the tides."
He said then the visitors had a different view of conservation, taking not just pāua but all sorts of other shellfish and octopus, and even scraping rocks clear of limpets.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/voyager-1: NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft has become the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth. It passed the milestone on 18 November 2026.

A light-day is how far light travels in a whole day. Voyager 1 is now about 26 billion kilometres away, more than four times as far as Pluto is from the Sun. That means a signal sent from Earth takes 24 hours to reach the spacecraft.

Voyager 1 is about the size of a small car and launched from Florida, in the United States, on 5 September 1977. Along the way, it photographed Jupiter, Saturn and Titan, which is Saturn’s largest moon.

In 1990, it took 64 pictures that together made the first “family portrait” of the solar system. In 2012, it moved beyond the reach of the Sun’s magnetic field and into interstellar space, which is the space between stars.
The spacecraft has lasted far longer than anyone expected, but eight of its 10 science instruments no longer work. Within the next ten years, scientists may receive its very last signal.
For now, Voyager 1 is still sending back information about space beyond our solar system. Next year, it and its twin, Voyager 2, will both have been in space for 50 years.
Pānui: Kua tae a Voyager 1 ki te tawhiti o te light-day kotahi i Papatūānuku
Ko te waka ātea a NASA, a Voyager 1, te mea tuatahi i hangaia e te tangata kua tae ki te tawhiti o te light-day kotahi i Papatūānuku. I tae atu ia ki taua tohu i te 18 o Noema 2026.

Ko te light-day te tawhiti e haere ai te marama i te roanga o te rā katoa. Kei te tata ki te 26 piriona kiromita te tawhiti o Voyager 1 i tēnei wā, neke atu i te whā whakareatanga o te tawhiti o Pluto i te Rā. Nō reira, e 24 hāora te roa kia tae atu tētahi tohu i tukuna mai i Papatūānuku ki te waka ātea.

He rite te rahi o Voyager 1 ki tētahi motukā iti, ā, i whakarewaina mai i Florida, i Amerika, i te 5 o Hepetema 1977. I tōna haerenga, i tango whakaahua ia o Hupita, o Hatana, me Titan, te marama nui rawa o Hatana.

I te tau 1990, i tango ia i ngā whakaahua e 64, ā, i hanga ngātahi ai te “whakaahua whānau” tuatahi o te pūnaha o te Rā. I te tau 2012, i haere ia ki tua atu o te papa autō o te Rā, ki te ātea i waenganui i ngā whetū.

Kua roa ake te ora o te waka ātea i tā te katoa i whakaaro ai, engari kua kore e mahi ngā taputapu pūtaiao e waru o ōna taputapu e 10. I roto i ngā tau tekau e heke mai nei, tērā pea ka whiwhi ngā kaipūtaiao i tōna tohu whakamutunga rawa.
I tēnei wā, kei te tuku mai tonu a Voyager 1 i ngā mōhiohio mō te ātea i tua atu o tō tātou pūnaha o te Rā. Ā tērā tau, ka 50 tau a ia me tōna māhanga, a Voyager 2, e noho ana i te ātea.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/leaders-o: US President Donald Trump, China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin are holding their first-ever three-way meeting. The talks are taking place on 19 November 2026 in Shenzhen, China.
The meeting is happening alongside Apec, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. Apec is a big gathering of countries in the region that meet to talk about trade.
No one knows exactly what the leaders will discuss in private, but there are some big issues affecting all three countries.
The war between the US and Israel on one side and Iran on the other has hurt economies around the world. China is the biggest buyer of Iran’s oil.
The US and China are also racing to become the world leader in artificial intelligence, or AI.

Russia has been more cut off from other countries since it invaded Ukraine in 2022. Experts think a breakthrough on ending that war is unlikely. European leaders, and especially Ukraine, are worried about talks that don’t include anyone from Ukraine.

Vladimir Putin has led Russia since 1999, sometimes as President and sometimes as Prime Minister. Donald Trump began his second term as US President in 2025, after first serving from 2017 to 2021. Xi Jinping has been China’s leader since 2012.
BBC China Correspondent Laura Bicker said the meeting is a chance for President Xi to show China as a bridge between big countries.
Details of what the three leaders agree on, if anything, are expected once the talks are over.
Pānui: Ka hui ngā kaiārahi o Amerika, Haina me Rūhia mō te wā tuatahi

Kei te hui tahi te Perehitini o Amerika, a Donald Trump, te Perehitini o Haina, a Xi Jinping, me te Perehitini o Rūhia, a Vladimir Putin, mō te wā tuatahi rawa. Kei te tū te hui i te 19 o Noema 2026 ki Shenzhen, i Haina.
Kei te tū te hui i te taha o Apec, arā, te Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. He hui nui a Apec mā ngā whenua o tēnei rohe hei kōrero mō te hokohoko.
Kāore tētahi e mōhio pū ki ngā kōrero a ngā kaiārahi i tā rātou hui tūmataiti, engari he take nui kei te pā ki ngā whenua e toru.
Kua raru ngā ōhanga huri noa i te ao i te pakanga i waenganui i Amerika me Iharaira i tētahi taha, me Iran i tērā taha. Ko Haina te kaihoko nui rawa o te hinu o Iran.
Kei te whakataetae hoki a Amerika rāua ko Haina kia noho ko rātou te kaiārahi o te ao mō te atamai hangahanga, arā, te AI.

Kua noho mokemoke ake a Rūhia i ētahi atu whenua mai i tana whakaeke i Ūkareina i te tau 2022. E whakaaro ana ngā tohunga kāore pea e kitea he huarahi hou hei whakamutu i taua pakanga. Kei te māharahara ngā kaiārahi o Ūropi, otirā a Ūkareina, mō ngā hui kāore he tangata nō Ūkareina e uru ana.

Kua ārahi a Vladimir Putin i a Rūhia mai i te tau 1999, i ētahi wā hei Perehitini, i ētahi wā hei Pirimia. I tīmata a Donald Trump i tana wāhanga tuarua hei Perehitini o Amerika i te tau 2025, i muri i tana wāhanga tuatahi mai i te tau 2017 ki te tau 2021. Ko Xi Jinping te kaiārahi o Haina mai i te tau 2012.
E ai ki te kaikawe kōrero o te BBC i Haina, a Laura Bicker, he whai wāhitanga tēnei hui mā te Perehitini Xi ki te whakaatu i a Haina hei arawhiti i waenganui i ngā whenua nunui.
Ā muri i te hui, ka mōhiotia ngā mea i whakaaetia e ngā kaiārahi e toru, mēnā he mea i whakaaetia.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/study-fin: If your cat keeps meowing at you, it might be asking for a hand. A new study from the University of São Paulo in Brazil has found that cats use meows, along with eye contact, to ask their owners for help.

The researchers visited 38 cats in their own homes. Each cat was given a treat trapped inside a small plastic box with holes in it, so it could see and smell the snack but couldn’t get it out by itself.

When a person was in the room, the cats meowed 85 times, compared with just 20 times when they were alone. That’s about four times as many. Overall, the cats were 16 times more likely to meow when a human was around.

With no person nearby, the cats mostly stayed quiet, stood still and stared at the door. When a person was there, the cats meowed while looking straight at them, and kept glancing back and forth between the human and the box.
The researchers also found that feral cats meow much less than pet cats. Feral cats live on their own and don’t belong to anyone.
The study was published in the journal Animal Behaviour . It says meowing isn’t just a cat showing how it feels. It plays a “communicative role”, which means it’s a way for cats to talk to people.
So next time your cat meows and stares at you, it may simply be asking for a little help.

Mēnā ka miau tonu tō ngeru ki a koe, tērā pea kei te tono āwhina ia. Kua kitea e tētahi rangahau hou nā te University of São Paulo i Parīhi, ka miau ngā ngeru, ka titiro hoki ki ngā kanohi, hei tono āwhina i ō rātou rangatira.

I toro atu ngā kairangahau ki ngā ngeru e 38 i ō rātou ake kāinga. I hoatu he kai reka ki ia ngeru, kua mau i roto i tētahi pouaka kirihou iti he kōputaputa ōna. Ka kite, ka hongi te ngeru i te kai, engari kāore e taea e ia anake te tango mai.

I te wā he tangata i roto i te rūma, e 85 ngā miau a ngā ngeru, engari e 20 noa iho i te wā i a rātou anake. Tata ki te whā whakareatanga te nui ake. Ina whakarāpopotohia, e 16 whakareatanga te nui ake o te tūponotanga ka miau ngā ngeru mēnā he tangata kei reira.

Ki te kore he tangata i te taha, i noho wahangū te nuinga o ngā ngeru, i tū mārie, ā, i titiro atu ki te kūaha. I te wā he tangata kei reira, i miau ngā ngeru me te titiro tika atu ki taua tangata, ā, i huri haere tō rātou titiro i waenganui i te tangata me te pouaka.
I kitea anō e ngā kairangahau he iti ake te miau a ngā ngeru mohoao i tō ngā ngeru mōkai. Ka noho motuhake ngā ngeru mohoao, ehara i te mōkai a tētahi.

I tāngia te rangahau ki te hautaka Animal Behaviour . E ai ki te rangahau, ehara te miau i te whakaatu noa a te ngeru i ōna kare-ā-roto. He “tūranga whakawhitiwhiti kōrero” tōna, arā, he huarahi mā ngā ngeru hei kōrero ki te tangata.
Nō reira, ā muri ake nei, ina miau tō ngeru me te titiro mai ki a koe, tērā pea kei te tono āwhina noa iho ia.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/bee-swarm: Auckland is seeing about twice as many bee swarms as usual this spring, with local beekeepers getting up to 10 calls for help a day.
Ken Brown, president of the Auckland Beekeepers Club, said the milder winter was the reason. He said the swarms had started about four weeks earlier than normal.
A swarm happens when a hive gets too crowded. The bees raise a new queen, and the old queen flies off with up to half the colony to start a new home somewhere else.
Brown said this is natural and “a sign of a good, strong, healthy hive”. In one backyard, thousands of bees turned up at once.

Phil Lester, a biology professor at Victoria University, said bees had been breeding well and growing their numbers. He said bees are important because they pollinate many of the crops we grow for food.
Swarms are being spotted all over New Zealand, and experts think swarming season could last until January.
Brown said swarms are not much of a risk to people, even if they can be a surprise to see in the city.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/darth-vad: A lightsaber used by Darth Vader in two Star Wars films has sold for US$4.875 million, making it the most expensive Star Wars item ever sold at auction.
The lightsaber was used in The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi. It appeared in the famous duel in Cloud City, where Darth Vader tells Luke Skywalker, “I am your father.”
It was sold by Heritage Auctions in the United States, at an event called the Ultimate Star Wars Auction. In an auction, people bid against each other, and whoever offers the most money wins.
The sale beat the old record, set in July, when Luke Skywalker’s lightsaber sold for US$3.75 million. That means Vader’s lightsaber went for more than US$1 million extra.
The auction also included 27 other lightsabers, along with items from all nine main Star Wars films and other movies and TV shows.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/des-bucki: New Zealand Football has confirmed Des Buckingham as the new head coach of the All Whites, New Zealand’s men’s football team, starting on 1 July 2027 and continuing through to the 2030 FIFA World Cup.
Buckingham will also lead the New Zealand Men’s Under-23 team as they aim to qualify for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games.

He is not new to New Zealand football. Buckingham lived and worked here for seven years, including as an assistant coach with the All Whites and head coach of the Men’s Under-23 side. In 2019, he guided that team to qualification for the Tokyo 2020 Olympics and to New Zealand’s first-ever Pacific Games football gold medal.
That same year, he led the Men’s Under-20 team to the country’s highest-ever finish at a men’s FIFA World Cup tournament, including a record 5-0 win over Honduras.

Since then, Buckingham has coached around the world, most recently as head coach of Al-Kholood in Saudi Arabia. He also led English club Oxford United into the Championship division for the first time in 25 years.
New Zealand Football chief executive Andrew Pragnell said the appointment was a big moment for the sport.
“I’m incredibly proud to announce Des as the new All Whites Coach,” Pragnell said. “This is huge for New Zealand Football and the future success of both NZF and the All Whites.”
Fans will have to wait until next July to see Buckingham take charge.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/new-parki: From December, visitors will have to pay to park at some of New Zealand’s most popular outdoor spots, as the Department of Conservation (DOC) rolls out paid parking more widely.
Sites getting paid car parks include Goat Island north of Auckland, the Tasman Glacier, Kura Tāwhiti/Castle Hill, the Routeburn Divide, and the Kepler Track control gates, among others.

At most of these places, the cost will be $2.50 for every half hour, or $20 for the whole day. At Goat Island, the first 10 minutes are free for quick drop-offs and pick-ups, and there is a separate $15 daily rate over winter.

People who live nearby can buy a $10 annual permit instead, which covers unlimited parking all year for up to two vehicles. School groups, DOC volunteers and community groups will be able to apply for an exemption.
The new fees follow a trial that started in the South Island earlier this year, at places like Punakaiki’s Pancake Rocks, Franz Josef and Aoraki Mount Cook.
David Butt, DOC’s director of heritage and visitors, said the money raised, expected to be about $3 million over the next year, would help look after the sites.
“We will use paid parking to generate revenue to contribute to the long-term care of places like Goat Island,” he said.

Cameras will keep track of cars coming in and out, and anyone who doesn’t pay could be issued a $75 breach notice – so if your family is planning a summer trip to one of these spots, it might pay to bring some extra coins.

The kauri tree is one of New Zealand’s most famous native trees. It can live for hundreds of years and grow to an enormous height. Scientists and conservation workers are studying a disease that affects kauri roots and can eventually kill the tree. This report explains what the disease is, how it spreads, and what people can do to help protect kauri forests. Readers are encouraged to clean their shoes before entering forest areas so soil is not carried from place to place. By following these steps, everyone can help keep kauri trees healthy for the future.
https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/robert-pa: British actor Robert Pattinson has been announced as the next James Bond, becoming the seventh actor to play the famous spy in the 64-year-old film series.
Amazon MGM Studios shared the news with a short video clip showing Pattinson, 40, stepping out of the shadows holding a gun, the character’s classic pose.
Pattinson is well known for playing Edward Cullen in the Twilight films, Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter, and the title role in The Batman. He is currently filming the sequel, The Batman Part II.
“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement.

The new film, known for now simply as “Bond 26,” will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, who also directed the Dune films. “I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond,” Villeneuve said.

Filming is expected to begin next year. It will be the first Bond film made since Amazon bought the MGM film studio in 2022, and the first where the Broccoli family, who have led the franchise for decades, haven’t personally chosen the lead actor.

The Bond films, based on novels by Ian Fleming, have earned more than US$7 billion at the box office since the first film in 1962. Fans will have to wait a while yet to see Pattinson in action as 007.
